For those who decided that direct computation is a good idea: 
Divide the whole set  $S = \{a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n\}$  of reals into four groups: the large and small negatives, and the large/small positives (while ignoring the zeroes because they're meaningless),
\[ N_l = \{x \mid x < -1 \}, N_{s} = \{ x \mid -1 \leq x < 0 \}\]
\[ P_l = \{x \mid x > 1 \}, P_s = \{ x \mid 0 < x \leq 1\} \]
We are going to count the value of  $\sum_{(i,j)\in A} a_ia_j$  =  $\frac{1}{2}\sum_{|a_i-a_j| \geq 1} a_ia_j$  according to each  $a_i$  (the front term), cycling one-by-one from the terms in  $N_l$  and  $P_l$  into  $N_s$  and  $P_s$ ,
\begin{align*}
\sum_{j, |n_l - a_j| \geq 1} n_l a_j & \leq \sum_{j} n_l a_j 
&\leq n_l \cdot (-n_l) = -n_l^2.
\end{align*}
Summing through all  $n_l$  and  $p_l$  (if indeed they are nonempty) -- we get 
\[ \sum_{\substack{|a_i-a_j| \geq 1  a_i \in N_l \cup P_l}} a_ia_j \leq - \sum_{a \in N_l \cup P_l} a^2\]
However, the  $a_i$  in the "small sets" needs to be handled more delicately. The important observation preceding the computation is that each  $a_i$  in, say  $N_s$ , cannot make  $\textbf{too much positive terms}$ , where it can only do so with terms from  $N_l$ , whence it  $\textbf{must make LARGE negative terms}$  with  $\textbf{ALL}$  terms of  $P_l$ . 
Formally, as we fix a  $a_i = n_s$ , and summing through all  $n_s$  and  $p_s$ , we get:
\begin{align*}
\sum_{j,|n_s-a_j| \geq 1} n_s a_j &\leq \sum_{j, a_j \in N_l \cup P_l} n_sa_j, 
&\leq n_s (-\sum_{a_j \in N_s \cup P_s}a_j),
\sum_{\substack{a_i \in N_s \cup P_s  |a_i - a_j| \geq 1}} a_ia_j &\leq -(\sum_{a\in N_s \cup P_s}a)^2 
\end{align*}
And we are done with the problem. Note that equality cannot be attained as the two statements " $N_l \cup P_l$  nonempty" (equality on first ineq) and "there does not exist  $a_i \in N_s, a_j \in P_s$  so that  $|a_i-a_j| \geq 1$ " (the terms we throw out on the second ineq) cannot be true simultaneously, making the right hand side definitely negative.

Note that $a_1 +...+ a_{n-k-1} = -(a_{n-k} +...+ a_n)$ . Now, if we order all of the  $|a_i - a_j|$  from highest to lowest, then we need to prove that for all  $X$  the sum of products of the pairs which make up the top  $X$  of these differences has to be smaller than  $0$ . Note that if no differences between the numbers with indices greater than or equal to  $n-k$  are counted,
then the total is always negative, as if any positive differences with smallest index  $z$  are used, then all of the differences between the negative numbers and the positive numbers are also used, which adds  $(a_{n-k} +...+ a_n)a_z = -(a_1+...+a_{n-k-1})a_z$  to the total, but adds a positive number of at most  $a_z(a_{z+1}+...+a_{n-k-1}) < (a_1+...+a_{n-k-1})a_z$ .

Now, we claim that given an  $a_y$ , with  $y \geq n-k$ , the total positive sum from everything used from the numbers with index  $n-k-1$  or smaller added to the sum of every negative
product used containing  $a_y$  is less than  $\frac{(a_1+...+a_{n-k-1}+a_y)^2}{2}$ .
We want that  $\frac{(a_1+...+a_{n-k-1}+a_y)^2}{2} > a_{y}(a_1+...+a_x) + a_x(a_{x+1}+...+a_{n-k-1}) + a_{x-1}(a_{x}+...+a_{n-k-1}) +...+ a_1(a_2+...+a_{n-k-1})$ , as
if the smallest difference containing  $a_y$  is  $|a_y - a_x|$ , then only the differences containing a number with index smaller than  $x$  can possibly be larger than this difference,
so the right hand side is the maximum possible sum.
However, after expanding the right hand side, some terms cancel; we are left with  $\frac{(a_1)^2+...+(a_{n-k-1})^2 + (a_y)^2}{2} + \sum_{i,j > x, i \neq j} [a_ia_j] +  a_y(a_1+...+a_{n-k-1} > a_y(a_1 +...+ a_x) \iff \frac{(a_1)^2+...+(a_{n-k-1})^2}{2} + \sum_{i,j > x, i \neq j} [a_ia_j] > a_y(-a_{x+1}-...-a_{n-k-1} - \frac{a_y}{2}) = \frac{a_y(-2a_{x+1} -...- 2a_{n-k-1} - a_y)}{2} = \frac{-a_y(2a_{x+1}+...+2a_{n-k-1} - (-a_y)}{2}$ . Since both of the numbers in the product are positive (or the second term is negative and the first term is positive, in which case the  $RHS$  is less than  $0$  but the  $LHS$  is greater than  $0$ , so we would be done), by AM-GM since the sum of the two numbers in the product doesn't depend on  $a_y$ , the maximum value of the  $RHS$  is when  $-a_y = 2a_{x+1} +...+ 2a_{n-k-1} -(-a_y) \implies a_y = -(a_{x+1} +...+ a_{n-k-1}$ .

Now, if we bring this back to the original expression, then we get that we need  $\frac{(a_1 +...+ a_x)^2}{2} > -(a_{x+1} +...+ a_{n-k-1})(a_1+...+a_x) + a_x(a_{x+1}+...+a_{n-k-1}) + a_{x-1}(a_{x}+...+a_{n-k-1}) +...+ a_1(a_2+...+a_{n-k-1}) = \sum_{i,j < x, i \neq j} [a_ia_j]$ . However, the  $LHS$  is equal to  $\sum_{i,j < x, i \neq j} [a_ia_j] + \frac{(a_1)^2 +...+ (a_x)^2}{2}$ ,
so since squares are always positive, the claim is proven.

Now, let  $Z = \{z_1,...,z_j\}$  be the set of indices greater than  $n-k-1$  for which at least one difference is used where  $z \in Z$  is the larger index, and the smaller index is also larger than  $n-k-1$ . Then the maximum possible sum is when every such difference is used. However, also note that for  $z$  to be an element of  $Z$ , we need that all of the differences between $a_z$  and a positive number have to be used, so we can add  $a_z(a_1+...+a_{n-k-1}) = -a_z(a_{n-k}+...+a_n)$  to the sum, and all the positive numbers we need to add are $a_za_{z-1} +...+ a_za_{n-k}$ , so the total amount we add is  $-a_z(a_z+...+a_n)$ . Therefore, we just need at any point that the sum of the other numbers used is smaller than $\sum_{i=1}^{i=j}[a_{z_i}(a_{z_i}+...+a_n)]$ . However, note that the same argument in the claim works for multiple  $a_i$ , if we change  $x$  to be the largest index used in a difference containing the smallest index used greater than  $n-k-1$  (this is weaker than the original claim as there may be some negative products that the original claim doesn't take into account  which are added to the right hand side, as the difference between an  $a_i$  with a larger index and  $a_{x+1}$  may be larger than the difference between the smallest index and  $a_x$ , thus making the right hand side smaller than in the claim, so it is definitely true). Therefore, if we let  $W = \{w_1,...,w_{n-k-j}\}$  be  $\{n-k,...,n\} - Z$ , then we have that the maximum possible sum of everything used which isn't in  $Z$  is
smaller than  $\frac{(a_1+...+a_{n-k-1} + \sum_{w \in W} [a_w])^2}{2} = \frac{(\sum_{z \in Z} [a_z])^2}{2}$ . However, now we are done,
as we want that  $\sum_{i=1}^{i=j}[a_{z_i}(a_{z_i}+...+a_n)] \geq \sum_{z \in Z} [\frac{(a_z)^2}{2}] + \sum_{i,j \in Z, i \neq j} [a_ia_j]$ , which is true as squares are always positive.</details>

stem_md: You are given a set of  $n$  blocks, each weighing at least  $1$ ; their total weight is  $2n$ . Prove that for every real number  $r$  with  $0 \leq r \leq 2n-2$  you can choose a subset of the blocks whose total weight is at least  $r$  but at most  $r + 2$ .
solution_md:
A unique solution:

Let the weight of the blocks be  $a_1 \leq a_2 \leq \cdots \leq a_n$ . Note that  $a_i \leq 2$  and  $a_n \geq 2$ . Further, let  $S=\{a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n\}$  denote the set of blocks, and for a subset  $A$  of  $S$  denote  $W(A)$  as the weight of the blocks in  $A$ . We prove the following lemma first:**Lemma:** There does not exist a positive integer  $1 \leq i \leq n$  such that  $a_i > 2+\sum_{k=1}^{i-1} a_k$ .**Proof:** Noting that for all  $k$ ,  $a_k \geq 1$ , we see that it suffices to show that there does not exist  $i$  such that  $a_i > 2+(i-1) \implies a_i > i+1$ . If such an  $i$  exists, then the sum of all the weights is strictly greater than  $(i-1)\cdot1+(n+1-i)\cdot(i+1)=n(i+1)+3i-i^2$ . We can see that this is at least  $2n$ , since  $n$  is a positive integer and  $1 \leq i \leq n$  (the inequality reduces to  $n(i-1)\geq i(i-3)$  after some straightforward computation, which holds if  $i,n$  satisfy the given constraints). Therefore, if such an  $i$  exists, then the sum of all of the weights must be strictly greater than  $2n$ , which is a contradiction. Therefore such an  $i$  does not exist, as desired.  $\blacksquare$ Call an interval *empty* if there does not exist a subset of the blocks whose total weight lies in the interval. Suppose for the sake of contradiction that an interval  $[r,r+2]$  with  $0 \leq r \leq 2n-2$  is empty.

We claim this supposition implies that, for all  $1 \leq k \leq n$ , there are no subsets of  $S \setminus \{a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_k\}$  which have a total weight in  $[r-s(k),r+2]$  where  $s(k)$  is defined as  $\sum_{i=1}^k a_k$ . We will prove this by induction on  $k$ .

Our base case is  $k=1$ . We know that  $[r,r+2]$  must be empty. Now consider any subset  $A$  of  $S \setminus \{a_1\}$ . If  $W(A) \in [r,r+2]$ , then it follows that  $[r,r+2]$  is not empty, so this cannot happen. Further, if  $W(A) \in [r-a_1,r]$ , then we have  $W(A \cup a_1) \in [r,r+a_1]$ . Since  $a_1 \leq 2$ , it follows that  $[r,r+a_1] \subseteq [r,r+2]$ , which would imply that  $[r,r+2]$  is not empty, so this cannot happen either. Therefore any subset of  $S \setminus \{a_1\}$  cannot fall in the interval  $[r-a_1,r+2]$ , which proves the base case.

Now for the inductive step. Suppose there are no subsets of  $S \setminus \{a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_{k-1}\}$  which have a total weight in  $[r-s(k-1),r+2]$ . Now consider any subset  $A$  of  $S \setminus \{a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_k\}$ . If  $W(A) \in [r-s(k-1),r+2]$ , then we reach a contradiction, since  $A$  is also a subset of  $S \setminus \{a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_{k-1}\}$ , yet has a total weight in  $[r-s(k-1),r+2]$ . If  $W(A) \in [r-s(k-1)-a_k,r-s(k-1)]$ , then we have  $W(A \cup a_k) \in [r-s(k-1),r-s(k-1)+a_k]$ . From our lemma, we know that  $a_k-s(k-1) \leq 2$ , so  $[r-s(k-1),r-s(k-1)+a_k] \subseteq [r-s(k-1),r+2]$ . But since  $A \cup a_k$  is a subset of  $S \setminus \{a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_{k-1}\}$ , this is a contradiction as well. Therefore, there are no subsets of  $S \setminus \{a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_k\}$  which have a total weight in  $[r-s(k),r+2]$ . This completes the inductive step, proving the claim.

Using this claim, we see that taking  $k=n$  shows that there are no subsets of  $S \setminus \{a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n\}=\emptyset$  which have a total weight in  $[r-s(n),r+2]=[r-2n,r+2]$ . But since  $r \geq 0$  and  $r \leq 2n$ ,  $[r-2n,r+2]$  contains  $0$ . Therefore, the claim implies that  $W(\emptyset)$  cannot be equal to  $0$ , which is absurd. Thus, our original supposition that an empty interval  $[r,r+2]$  exists cannot be true. This implies the desired result.  $\blacksquare$

WLOG $w(1) \le w(2) \le w(3) \le \cdots \le w(n)$ **Claim.** $w(k) \le k + 1$ *Proof. *Assume the contrary for some $1 \le k \le n$ . We have $$ 2n = w(1) + w(2) + \cdots + w(n) > k - 1 + (n - k + 1)(k + 1) = 2n + (n - k)(k - 1) $$ Hence, we have $0 > (n - k)(k - 1)$ , but clearly both terms are always nonnegative, absurd $\square$ Clearly this implies $w(n) < w(1) + w(2) + w(3) + \cdots + w(n - 1) + 2$ . Now define a $N-\text{chain}$ to be all checkpoints consisting of blocks $w(1), w(2), w(3), \cdots , w(N)$ . **Claim. ** All such $N-\text{chains}$ satisfy the revised condition. *Proof. * Proceed via induction. **Solution.** We prove the following.
You are given a set of $n$ blocks, each weighing at least $1$ ; their total weight is $s\leq 2n$ . Prove that for every real number $r$ with $0 \leq r \leq s-2$ you can choose a subset of the blocks whose total weight is at least $r$ but at most $r + 2$ .
For every $r$ we color the interval $[r,r+2]$ . The question is now equivalent to proving the interval $[0,s]$ is colored. For $n=1$ , it is evident. Assume it's true for $n=k$ . Consider $k+1$ blocks. In the worst-case scenario, the sum is $2(k+1)$ , and thus by the pigeonhole principle, there is a block with sum $\ge 2$ and consequently, there is a subset of $k$ blocks that sums $\leq 2k$ . Consider $k+1$ blocks, $a_1,\dots, a_{k+1}$ . By the previous reasoning, we can assume $s'=a_1 + \dots + a_k \leq 2k$ . Any $r\in [0,s']$ works by induction hypothesis (The induction hypothesis shows that it's true for $r \in [0,s'-2]$ , but we can extend to $[0,s']$ since we can choose $s'$ ). It's enough to show $r\in [s',s'+a_{k+1}-2]$ also works. We do some casework.**1. $a_{k+1} \leq 2$** Then for any $r\in [s',s'+a_{k+1}-2]$ , we choose the number $s'+a_{k+1}=a_1+\dots+a_{k+1}$ .**2. $a_{k+1} > 2$** We want to prove that we can choose any $r \in [0,(s'+a_{k+1})-2]$ or in other words the interval $[0,s'+a_{k+1}]$ is colored. Note that since $[0,s'-2]$ works by the induction hypothesis, $[0,s']$ is colored. So we show that $[s',s'+a_{k+1}]$ is colored.**2a. $s'=a_{k+1}$** For any $0 \leq \epsilon \leq s' -2$ . There is a subset whose sum lies on $[\epsilon, \epsilon+2]$ . Add that with $a_{k+1}$ so the subset sum lies on $$ [\epsilon+a_{k+1}, \epsilon+2+a_{k+1}] $$ $$ [\epsilon+s', \epsilon+2+s'] $$ Note that as $\epsilon$ varies in $[0,s'-2]$ , the interval $[s',2s']=[s',s'+a_{k+1}]$ is coloured.**2b. $s' > a_{k+1}$** Take $r=s'-a_{k+1}+\epsilon$ where $0\leq \epsilon \leq a_{k+1}$ and thus $s'-a_{k+1} \leq r \leq s'$ . The sum lies between $$ [s'-a_{k+1}+\epsilon,s'-a_{k+1}+\epsilon+2] $$ Now we add the $a_{k+1}$ block, so the sum lies in $$ [s'+\epsilon, s'+\epsilon +2] $$ Note that as $\epsilon$ varies in $[0,a_{k+1}]$ , the interval $[s',s'+a_{k+1}+2]$ is colored. **2c.** $a_{k+1} > s' \ge 1+\dots+1 = k$ $$ 2s' < a_{k+1}+s' \leq 2k+2 \implies s' < k+1 $$ So $k \leq s' < k+1$ $$ a_{k+1}+k \leq a_{k+1}+s' \leq 2k+2 \implies a_{k+1} \leq k+2 $$ So, $k \leq a_{k+1}\leq k+2$ And so we have that $a_{k+1}-s'\leq 2$ . Note that $r \in [0,s']$ is covered by the hypothesis. $r\in [s,a_{k+1}]$ is covered by taking $a_{k+1}$ . Now we show $r\in [a_{k+1},a_{k+1}+s'-2]$ is covered or $[a_{k+1},a_{k+1}+s']$ is colored. Take $\epsilon \in [0,s'-2]$ . The subset sum lies on $$ [\epsilon,\epsilon +2] $$ Add the $a_{k+1}$ $$ [a_{k+1}+\epsilon, a_{k+1}+\epsilon+2] $$ So $[a_{k+1},a_{k+1}+s']$ is colored.

We induct on $n.$ The base case is obvious, now suppose it is true for $n,$ and consider $n+1$ blocks with total weight $2n+2.$ Call the lightest block *anorexic* and the heaviest block *american.* **Claim:** For $2n-2 < r \le 2n,$ it is possible. *Proof.* If $2n-1\le r\le 2n,$ remove the anorexic block and you are done. Suppose that $2n-2< r < 2n-1.$ If the weight of the anorexic block is 2, then remove the anorexic block and you are done. Thus, suppose anorexic block has weight strictly less than 2. - If there exists another block $B$ distinct from the anorexic one with weight $b\le 2,$ and if $r> 2n-b-w,$ then remove only $B.$ Otherwise remove both $B$ and the anorexic one. - If no other block has weight at most $2,$ then there must exist a block $B$ with weight at most $3$ and more than $2,$ otherwise the total sum would be strictly greater than $3n-2 \ge 2n,$ contradiction. Hence, remove block $B$ and you are done. [/list] Therefore, the result is true for $2n-1 < r \le 2n.$ $\blacksquare$ **Claim:** For $0\le r\le 2n-2,$ it is possible to find weights with sum in $[r, r+2]$ . *Proof.* Note that the american block has weight at least $2$ and the anorexic block has weight $w\le 2.$ Let $0\le \varepsilon = 2-w \le 1.$ Remove the anorexic block from the pile and subtract $\varepsilon$ from the american block (diet). Note that by assumption, for such given $r,$ there exists some subset $S$ of these remaining weights with sum in $[r-1, r+1].$ We first consider when $S$ has sum in $[r, r+1]:$ [list] - If the american block is in $S,$ then simply add $\varepsilon$ back and the weight of $S$ will be at most $r+2.$ - If the american blocks is not in $S,$ then a valid subset of the original blocks lies in $[r, r+2]$ and we're done. [/list] If $S$ has sum in $[r-1, r]:$ [list] - If the american block is not in $S$ , then simply add the anorexic block to $S$ and then we're done. - If the american block is in $S,$ then add $\varepsilon$ back to the american block and add the anorexic block, resulting in sum between $[r+1, r+2]$ so we're done. Hence, the claim is proven and we conclude by induction the problem is true. $\blacksquare$

Simple and elegant solution by Konstantin Knop: 

Replace the weight of blocks with the length of line segments, and arrange all the segments in a circle (the end of one corresponds to the beginning of the next, the order does not matter). Thus, we get  the following problem: "find a subset of segments of total length between  $r$  and  $r+2$ ".  Call the ends of the segments - the *blue dots*. Rotate all the blue dots by  $(r+1)$ . For example, clockwise, and call the new endpoints of the segments - the*red dots*. Since in total we have  $2n$  dots on a circle of length  $2n$ , the distance between a certain pair of dots is  $\le$  1. 

If it is strictly  $<1$ , these cannot be two dots of the same color (according to the fact that each segment is of length  $\ge 1$  ). This means that we have a blue dot (call it B1) and a red dot within the distance of  $1$ . (If the minimal distance is exactly  $=1$ , then there is still a pair of dots of different colors at a distance of  $1$ .) But since the red dot is exactly at the distance of  $(r+1)$  from its blue prototype (call it B2), the distance between the blue dots B1 and B2 differs from  $(r+1)$   by no more than 1 as required.

stem_md: Let  $m$  be a given positive integer. Prove that there exists a positive integer  $k$  such that it holds   $$ 1\leq \frac{1^m+2^m+3^m+\ldots +(k-1)^m}{k^m}<2. $$
solution_md:
Let  $S_k=1^m+2^m+...+(k-1)^m-k^m$ .It is enough to show that there exists positive integer  $k$  such that  $S_k\in [0,k^m)$ .

It is known that  $1^m+2^m+...+n^m$  is a  $m+1$  degree polynomial with positive leading coefficient .So letting  $k\to\infty$  there is  $N$  such that for all  $k\ge N$   $S_k$  is positive.Let  $r$  be the biggest integer such that  $S_r$  is negative.Note that  $S_2$  is negative.So such  $r$  exists.

Now  $S_{r+1}-S_r=2r^m-(r+1)^m<r^m$ .As  $S_{r+1}$  is positive and from the last inequality it is obvious that  $S_{r+1}\in[0,r^m)$ . $\blacksquare$

For the triple  $(a,b,c)$  of positive integers we say it is interesting if  $c^2+1\mid (a^2+1)(b^2+1)$  but none of the  $a^2+1, b^2+1$  are divisible by  $c^2+1$ . 
Let  $(a,b,c)$  be an interesting triple, prove that there are positive integers  $u,v$  such that  $(u,v,c)$  is interesting and  $uv<c^3$ .
solution_md:
At first note that for any prime  $p$  of the form  $4k+1$  and any negative integer  $a$  there is a residue  $x\ (mod p^a)$  such that  $x^2+1\equiv 0\ (mod\  p^a)$ .Indeed, for  $ a=1$  it is true.We can climb on higher powers of  $p$  by Hensel's lemma.

Now note that  $c^2+1$  can't be a prime otherwise it will devide at least one of  $a^2+1$  or  $b^2+1$ .So it must be composite.

If  $c^2+1$  is even note that  $4$  can't devide  $c^2+1$ .So let  $c=2p_1^{a_1}p_2^{a_2}...p_r^{a_r}$  where  $p_i's$  are prime of the form  $4k+1$ .Take  $u=1$ .Now we claim that there exists even  $x$  such that  $x<p_1^{a_1}p_2^{a_2}...p_r^{a_r}=(c^2+1)/2<c^2$  such that  $x^2+1\equiv 0\ (mod\ p_1^{a_1}p_2^{a_2}...p_r^{a_r})$ .Indeed there is $x_i^2\equiv -1\ (mod\ p_i^{a_i})$  for all  $i=1,2,...,r$ by Hensel  and so by CRT there is  $x (mod\ p_1^{a_1}p_2^{a_2}...p_r^{a_r})$  which satisfy the equation.Now if  $x$  is even we take  $v=x$  otherwise take  $v=p_1^{a_1}p_2^{a_2}...p_r^{a_r}-x$ .Take  $u=1$ .Ofcourse  $(u,v,c)$  is a interesting triple.

Now let  $c^2+1= odd=p_1^{a_1}p_2^{a_2}...p_r^{a_r}$  where all the primes are of the form  $4k+1$ .Now at least one prime divisior of  $c^2+1$  will be less than  $c$ .Let this prime be  $p_1$ .There is  $x<p_1<c$  such that  $x^2+1\equiv 0\ (mod\ p_1)$ .
Now we claim that there exists  $y<(c^2+1)/p_1<c^2$  such that  $y^2+1\equiv 0( mod\ (c^2+1)/p_1)$  and  $y^2+1\not=0\ (mod\ c^2+1)$ .
At first note that if  $p^{a_1-1}|y^2+1$  and  $p^{a_1}|y^2+1$  then  $(y-p^{a_1-1})^2+1\not=0(mod\ p^{a_1})$  and  $(y-p^{a_1-1})^2+1\equiv 0(mod\ p^{a_1-1})$   .And for all the other primes we can take  $y_i^2+1\equiv 0( mod\ p^{a_i})$  for all  $i=2,3,...r$ .So by CRT the claim is proved.
Now take  $u=x$  and  $v=y$ .We get  $(u,v,c)$  a interesting triple.

Here is a size solution.

Claim 1. If  $p\mid a_n, p\mid a_{n-1}+1$ .

Proof 1. We proceed by induction. The base case is trivial. If  $p\mid a_n=a_{n-2}(a_{n-1}+1)$ , either  $p\mid a_{n-1}+1$  or  $p\mid a_{n-2}$ . The first case is trivial. The second case follows from the inductive hypothesis; if  $p\mid a_{n-2}$ ,  $p\mid a_{n-3}+1$ , so  $p\mid a_{n-3}+a_{n-3}a_{n-2}+1=a_{n-1}+1$ .

We can also easily show  $a_n\equiv n(\bmod\; 2)$ , so  $a_{a_n}=a_{a_n-2} (a_{a_n-1}+1) =\cdots = a_n \prod\limits_{n<i<a_n, 2\nmid i-n} (a_i+1)$ .

Dividing both sides by  $a_n$ , we wish to show  $(a_n)^{n-1} \mid \prod\limits_{n<i<a_n, 2\nmid i-n} (a_i+1)$ .

By Claim 1, if  $p\mid a_n, p\mid a_i+1$  for all of these  $i$ . Hence  $\nu_p(RHS)=\frac{a_n-n}{2}$  and  $\nu_p(a_n^{n-1})=(n-1)\nu_p(a_n)<(n-1)\log_2(a_n)$ .

Claim 2:  $a_n\ge 2^n$  for all  $n>7$ .

We can verify this is true for  $n=6,7$ . For  $n>7, a_n=a_{n-2}(a_{n-1}+1)>2\cdot 2^{n-1}=2^n$ .

Therefore, since  $(n-1)\log_2(x)<<\frac{x-n}{2}$  for  $x\ge 2^n$ , we're done.

(1)  $\gcd(a_i,a_{i-1})=1$ (2)  $a_i\mid a_{i+2}$  so we can more easily relate  $a_{a_n}$  to  $a_n$ .

stem_md: $BB_1$  is the angle bisector of  $\triangle ABC$ , and  $I$  is its incenter. The perpendicular bisector of segment  $AC$  intersects the circumcircle of  $\triangle AIC$  at  $D$  and  $E$ . Point  $F$  is on the segment  $B_1C$  such that  $AB_1=CF$ .Prove that the four points  $B, D, E$  and  $F$  are concyclic.
solution_md:
Let  $BB_1$  meets the circumcircle of  $ABC$  again at  $X$ .  We know that  $X$  is the center of  $(AIC)$  that is the midpoint of  $DE$ . Assume that  $XF$  meets the circumcircle of  $ABC$  again at  $P$ . Then, the points  $B$  and  $P$ ,  $B_1$  and  $F$  are symmetrical with respect to the line  $DE$ . 

Considering an inversion centred at  $X$  with radius  $XI$ , we obtain that  $B\leftrightarrow B_1$ ,  $P\leftrightarrow F$  and the points  $B,C,D,E$  are fixed. So the circle  $(BDF)$  goes to the circle  $(PDB_1)$ . 

Let  $E'$  be the second intersection point of the circles  $(BDF)$  and  $(PDB_1)$ . As they are mapped each to other by the inversion, we get that  $E'$  should be fixed under the inversion, i.e.  $E'$  lies on  $(AIC)$ . On the other hand, the triangles  $BDF$  and  $PDB_1$  are symmetrical with respect to the line  $DE$ , so their circumcenters are too. That means  $DE$  be the radical axis of their circumcircles. Hence  $E\equiv E'$  and  $B$ ,  $D$ ,  $F$ ,  $E$  are concyclic.

stem_md:
$N$  oligarchs built a country with  $N$  cities with each one of them owning one city. In addition, each oligarch built some roads such that the maximal amount of roads an oligarch can build between two cities is  $1$  (note that there can be more than  $1$  road going through two cities, but they would belong to different oligarchs).
A total of  $d$  roads were built. Some oligarchs wanted to create a corporation by combining their cities and roads so that from any city of the corporation you can go to any city of the corporation using only corporation roads (roads can go to other cities outside corporation) but it turned out that no group of less than  $N$  oligarchs can create a corporation. What is the maximal amount that  $d$  can have?
solution_md:
The answer is  $\boxed{\binom{N}{3}}.$ We can achieve this as follows. Label the oligarchs  $1, 2, \cdots, N$  arbitrarily. For  $1 \le i \le N,$  let the  $i$ th oligarch build roads between the cities owned by oligarchs  $j$  and  $k$  for all  $1 <= j < k < i.$  

Then, for any set  $S$  of less than  $N$  oligarchs, it's clearly impossible to reach the city of the oligarch in  $S$  with the largest label from any city of the other oligarchs in  $S$ .  

Now, let's show that  $\binom{N}{3}$  is actually optimal. For  $N \le 3$  this can be easily verified. Suppose now that  $N \ge 4$ .

Notice that no oligarch can build a road adjacent to their city, as then the set of  $2$  oligarchs consisting of the endpoints of that road would violate the desired condition. Now, let's get an upper bound on the number of ordered triples  $(a, b, c)$  such that the oligarch  $a$  builds a road connecting the cities of oligarchs  $b$  and  $c.$  Call such triples **good.** Observe that this quantity is precisely twice the number of constructed roads, or  $2d$  (since if  $(a, b, c)$  is counted so is  $(a, c, b)$ ). 

Note that from our latest result,  $a, b, c$  must be distinct in any such triple. Now, notice that if  $(a, b ,c)$  and  $(b, a, c)$  are both good, the set of two oligarchs  $\{a, b\}$  violates the condition. This then yields that for each unordered triple  $(x, y, z)$  of distinct oligarchs, at most two out of the six permutations are good. Finally, we obtain that there are at most  $2 \binom{N}{3}$  good triples and so we're done, as this quantity is also exactly  $2d.$  $\square$

stem_md: Find all positive integers  $n$   such that the sum of the squares of the five smallest divisors of  $n$  is a square.
solution_md:
I think the question requires a condition that  $n$  has atleast  $5$  positive divisors :D
<details><summary>hopefully correct solution (:</summary>We claim that there is no such  $n$ .

Let  $1,d_2,d_3, d_4, d_5$  be the  $5$  smallest divisors of  $n$  in increasing order. $x^2=1+d_2^2+d_3^2+d_4^2+d_5^2$ If  $n$  is odd, then all  $d_i$  are odd and hence,  $x^2=RHS\equiv 5\pmod 8$ , not possible. So,  $d_2=2$ If  $4|n$ , then we take two cases 

- If  $3|n$ ,  $d_3=3,d_4=4$  gives  $x^2=30+d_5^2$  but this equation has no solution(just see mod 4)
- If  $3\nmid n$ , then  $d_3=4$ . Both  $d_4$  and  $d_5$  are even due to mod 4. But if  $d_4=2^ab$  where  $b$  is odd, then  $b|n$  and  $b<d_4$ , contradiction. So,  $d_4,d_5$  are powers of  $2$  and hence,  $x^2\equiv 3\pmod 4$ , not possible.

So,  $4\nmid n$  and hence  $d_3$  is an odd.
Both  $d_4$  and  $d_5$  must be odd, by  $\mod 4$ .
If  $d_3\geq 5$ ,  $x^2=5+d_3^2+d_4^2+d_5^2\equiv 2\pmod 6$ , not possible. 
So,  $d_3=3$ But,  $d_3=3\implies 6|n$  so one of  $d_4,d_5$  is  $6$ , contradiction to the fact that  $d_4,d_5$  are odd.
Hence, we have exhausted all cases and conclude that no such  $n$  exists.</details>
<details><summary>comment</summary>A shorter proof might be possible using  $\mod 12$ , but this seems a bit natural</details>

P.S. 5959th post :P

stem_md:
The points  $(1,1),(2,3),(4,5)$  and  $(999,111)$  are marked in the coordinate system. We continue to mark points in the following way : 


- If points  $(a,b)$  are marked then  $(b,a)$  and  $(a-b,a+b)$  can be marked
- If points  $(a,b)$  and  $(c,d)$  are marked then so can be  $(ad+bc, 4ac-4bd)$ .

Can we, after some finite number of these steps, mark a point belonging to the line  $y=2x$ .
solution_md:
The answer is no!

Proof. Consider the sum of the squares of coordinates of a point modulo  $5$ .

For points  $(a,b)$  and  $(b,a)$  the sum is  $a^2+b^2 \pmod{5}$ .

For point  $(a-b,a+b)$  the sum is  $2(a^2+b^2)$ .

For point  $(ad+bc,\,4ac-4bd)$  the sum is
\[
(ad+bc)^2+(4ac-4bd)^2 \equiv (a^2+b^2)(c^2+d^2)\pmod{5}.
\]

If a point  $P\in y=2x$ , then its coordinates are  $(x,2x)$ , which means that the sum of squares of its coordinates is  $x^2+(2x)^2\equiv 0 \pmod{5}$ .

For the initial points  $P_1,P_2,P_3,P_4$ ,  $x_P^{\,2}+y_P^{\,2}\not\equiv 0 \pmod{5}$ . Hence it is not possible.

stem_md:
On a social network, no user has more than ten friends ( the state "friendship" is symmetrical). The network is connected: if, upon learning interesting news a user starts sending it to its friends, and these friends to their own friends and so on, then at the end, all users hear about the news. 
Prove that the network administration can divide users into groups so that the following conditions are met:


- each user is in exactly one group
- each group is connected in the above sense
- one of the groups contains from  $1$  to  $100$  members and the remaining from  $100$  to  $900$ .
solution_md:
So, we have a connected graph  $G$  and have to partition its vertices into groups with corresponding sizes inducing connected subgraphs. Let  $T$  be a spanning tree of  $G$ . Then,  $\deg_T(v)\le 10$  for every vertex of  $T$ . Suppose  $u_0$  is a root of  $T$  and denote by  $V(v)$  the number of vertices of the the subtree of  $T$  consisting of  $v$  and all vertices of  $T$  upper than  $v$ . Taking a leef and proceeding down to  $u_0$  let  $v_0$  be the first vertex with  $V(v_0)>900$ . Then   $v_0$  is connected with at most  $9$  upward vertices  $v_i,i=1,2,\dots 9$ . If  $V(v_i)\leq 900$  for all  $i\in[1..9]$  we are done since  $V(v_i)\in[100,900]$  for some  $i$ . Otherwise we go up until we reach a vertex  $v_0$  with  $V(v_i)\leq 900$  for all vertices upper than  $v_0$ .
	Removing one by one subtrees with vertices from  $100$  to  $900$  and taking care at the end, we can reach the goal.

stem_md: Andryusha has  $100$  stones of different weight and he can distinguish the stones by appearance, but does not know their weight. Every evening, Andryusha can put exactly  $10$  stones on the table and at night the brownie will order them in increasing weight. But, if the drum also lives in the house then surely he will in the morning change the places of some  $2$  stones.Andryusha knows all about this but does not know if there is a drum in his house. Can he find out?
solution_md: Yes he can. Consider a 10-tuple ,call the changed pair (if it exists) *bad* and let $S$ be the set of the $100$ stones. Step_1 Let him consider $3$ disjoint $10$ -tuples $A, B$ and $C$ and have him note down all the greater-smaller relations as they occur after a night has passed. Step_2 Consider all 10-tuples of this type: $2$ stones from each of $A$ , $B$ and $C$ ( $6$ in total) and a fixed $4$ tuple from $S/ \{A,B,C\}$ . Have him do this so that all of the $\binom{10}{2} \binom{10}{2} \binom{10}{2}$ $6$ tuples occur in one such $10$ -tuple. This means that one of these $10$ -tuples must contain all $3$ bad pairs of $A$ , $B$ and $C$ , wlog $(a_1,a_2), (b_1,b_2), (c_1,c_2)$ , respectively. with $a_1a_2$ , $b_1>b_2$ , $c_1>c_2$ in the drums catalog and the one that the guy playing has noted down. Since , drum can only change $2$ of these $6$ stones one of these pairs remains for sure unchanged and hence $A$ has his notes contradicted. Which means there is a drum. If after the above procedure none of the notes he has written are contradicted, then the drum is not in his house.

stem_md: Rays  $\ell, \ell_1, \ell_2$  have the same starting point  $O$ , such that the angle between  $\ell$  and  $\ell_2$  is acute and the ray  $\ell_1$  lies inside this angle. The ray  $\ell$  contains a fixed point of  $F$  and an arbitrary point  $L$ . Circles passing through  $F$  and  $L$  and tangent to  $\ell_1$  at  $L_1$ , and passing through  $F$  and  $L$  and tangent to  $\ell_2$  at  $L_2$ . Prove that the circumcircle of  $\triangle FL_1L_2$  passes through a fixed point other than  $F$  independent on  $L$ .
solution_md: Note that  $OL_1^2 = OF \cdot OL = OL_2^2$ . So the circumcenter of  $FL_1L_2$  lies on the angle bisector of  $\ell_1, \ell_2$ . Thus the circumcircle of  $FL_1L_2$  passes through the reflection of  $F$  over the said angle bisector, and we are done.

stem_md:
Let  $G$  be a graph with  $400$  vertices. For any edge  $AB$  we call *a cuttlefish* the set of all edges from  $A$  and  $B$  (including  $AB$ ). Each edge of the graph is assigned a value of  $1$  or  $-1$ . It is known that the sum of edges at any cuttlefish is greater than or equal to  $1$ .
Prove that the sum of the numbers at all edges is at least  $-10^4$ .
solution_md:
Please tell me I'm not high

Choose the largest matching  $M = \{v_1-w_1,v_2-w_2,\dots v_n-w_n\}$  in the graph. Let  $N$  be the set of vertices not in  $M$ , then  $N$  is an independent set. If  $N = \emptyset$  then summing along edges  $v_iw_i$ , each edge's weight is counted twice except for those joining a pair in  $M$ , so the total edge sum is  $\ge \frac{n - n}{2} = 0 \ge 10^{-4}$ . From now on assume that  $N$  is nonempty, then  $|N| =400 - 2n \ge 2$ . Since there are no  $n_1, n_2 \in N$  and  $i \in \{1,\dots,n\}$  with  $v_1-v_i, v_2 - w_i$  it follows that for each edge  $v_iw_i$  the number of edges from  $N$  into  $v_iw_i$  is at most  $400-2n$ . Now we sum along the edges of the matching as before, the number of edges counted  $1\times$  is  $\le (401-2n)n$  so that the total sum of edge weights is   $$ \ge \frac{n-(401-2n)n}{2} = (n-200)n \ge -10^4, $$  as desired.

stem_md:
The exam has  $25$  topics, each of which has  $8$  questions. On a test, there are  $4$  questions of different topics.
Is it possible to make  $50$  tests so that each question was asked exactly once, and for any two topics there is a test where are questions of both topics?
solution_md:
Since  $1+3\cdot8=25$ , then we can label the topics  $0$  and then a combination of the numbers  $1$  through  $8$  with a letter from  $A$  to  $C$ . We will call these subtopics. Assume WLOG that the tests containing topic  $0$  are  $(0,1A,1B,1C)$  through  $(0, 8A, 8B, 8C)$ Now there are  $50-8=42$  tests remaining. Notice that two subtopics with the same number (topic) cannot appear on the remainder of these tests because they already did before

Notice that the problem essentially reduces down to the same problem but with  $8$  topics and  $14$  tests with  $4$  questions from different topics, with each pair of topics having exactly  $3$  tests they both appear in. This is because once we can find an example of this, then when we expand it to  $42$  tests, each pair of topics will have exactly  $9$  tests they both appear in, which happens to be exactly the same number of combination of subtopics two topics can have  $(3\cdot3)$ , so we can assign each test two topics have in common to a unique combination of subtopics

To do this, for the first two tests, assign then as topics  $(1,2,3,4)$  and  $(5,6,7,8)$ . For the other  $12$  tests, assign two tests for each possible combination of  $\binom42=6$  pairs of two topics out of the first four topics. If the topics are  $a,b$ , then assign the first test to have topics  $a+4, b+4$  and assign the other test to be the opposite. For example, the tests with topics  $(1,4)$  would be  $(1,4,5,8)$  and  $(1,4,6,7)$ This works because if topics  $x$  and  $y$  are both in the range from  $1-4$  or  $5-8$ , then we set up the tests so that there are exactly two in the first  $12$  that contain both  $x$  and  $y$ , and the one of the last two tests does as well, which gives us a total of three.

If one of them is in the range from  $1-4$  and other is in the range from  $5-8$ , then the first two tests do not contain both  $x$  and  $y$ . But by symmetry there are  $6$  tests in the first  $12$  that have topic  $x$ . We also set it up so that exactly half of them have topic  $y$ , as the other set of topics comes in pairs with complement each other. This gives us a total of three tests they have in common

Therefore, this construction works and we are done  $\blacksquare$

stem_md:
On a table with  $25$  columns and  $300$  rows, Kostya painted all its cells in three colors. Then, Lesha, looking at the table, for each row names one of the three colors and marks in that row all cells of that color (if there are no cells of that color in that row, he does nothing). After that, all columns that have at least a marked square will be deleted. 
Kostya wants to be left as few as possible columns in the table, and Lesha wants there to be as many as possible columns in the table. What is the largest number of columns Lesha can guarantee to leave?
solution_md:
Answer: 2

We first show that Lesha can always leave 2 columns. Select two arbitrary column. For each row, name a color which doesn't appear in the two cells in selected column of the row(there are at most 2 colors and Lesha  can name the other). Then, the selected two column leave after deletion. 

Next, Kostya can paint the table in such a way that Lesha cannot leave more than 2 columns. For each rows we label two element subset  $\{i, j\}$  of  $\{1,2,\ldots,25\}$  . There are exactly  $\binom{25}2 = 300$  subsets. Let the colors be  $A,B,C$ . For each row labeled  $\{i,j\}$ , we color  $i$ -th cell  $A$ ,  $j$ -th cell  $B$  and other cells  $C$ . Then, we show that Lesha cannot leave more than 2 columns. If Lesha name color  $C$ , for some row, only 2 columns left. Thus, Lesha must name  $A$  or  $B$  to each row. We assume three columns which is  $i,j,k$ -th column left. Consider the row with label  $\{i,j\}$ , the  $i,j,k$ -th cell in the row has three different colors. Thus, Lesha must mark at least one of these cells, a contradiction.

stem_md: Find all monic polynomials  $P(x)$  such that the polynomial  $P(x)^2-1$  is divisible by the polynomial  $P(x+1)$ .
solution_md:
Essentially the same as the solution given in the above link. Just for storage. The answer is the constant polynomial $P(x) = 1$ and the linear polynomials $P(x) = x + b$ for any $b \in \mathbb{Z}$ . The latter polynomial satisfies since $P(x + 1) = (x + b + 1)$ divides $P(x)^2 - 1 = (x + b)^2 - 1 = (x + b - 1)(x + b + 1) = (x + b - 1) P(x + 1)$ . We'll show that only these polynomials satisfy. First, the case of $\text{deg} (P(x)) \le 1$ are handled seperately. ----------------**Claim.** All roots of $P(x)$ are the same. *Proof.* Suppose that $P$ has degree $n \ge 2$ . Then, we could rewrite $P(x) = \prod_{i = 1}^n (x - z_i)$ where $z_i$ 's are the complex roots of $P$ . Now, WLOG $\text{Re}(z_1) \le \text{Re}(z_2) \le \dots \le \text{Re}(z_n)$ .
Why?Usually when we want to "order" the complex numbers, we could use the real part of the complex numbers to compare the two complex numbers instead to form some sort of ordering just like real numbers.
Therefore, we know that $|P(z_i - 1)| = 1$ for all complex root $z_i$ . Furthermore, we know that $\text{Re}(z_1 - z_i - 1) \le -1$
Why?Since we take $\text{Re}(z_1) \le \text{Re}(z_i)$ . Thus, $\text{Re}(z_1 - z_i) \le 0$ .
Why do we consider this?We want to evaluate $|P(z_i - 1)| = 1$ and by definition, we have a bunch of terms in form of $z_1 - z_i - 1$ . Furthermore, we know that for any complex number $z$ , we have $|z| = \sqrt{\text{Re}(z)^2 + \text{Im}(z)^2} \ge |\text{Re}(z)|$ .
Therefore, we know that $|z_1 - z_i - 1| \ge |\text{Re}(z_1 - z_i - 1)| \ge 1$ for all $1 \le i \le n$ . Now, we know that \[ 1 = |P(z_1 - 1)| = \left| \prod_{i = 1}^n (z_1 - 1 - z_i ) \right| = \prod_{i = 1}^n |z_1 - 1 - z_i| \ge \prod_{i = 1}^n 1 = 1 \] Therefore, equality must hold, which means that $|z_1 - z_i - 1| = 1$ for all complex root $z_i$ . This forces $z_1 = z_i$ for any $1 \le i \le n$ .
Why?We need to consider the cases when equality holds in the above inequality. First, it holds when $z_1 - z_i - 1 = \text{Re}(z_1 - z_i - 1)$ , in which $\text{Im}(z_1 - z_i) = \text{Im}(z_1 - z_i - 1) = 0$ , and $\text{Re}(z_1 - z_i - 1) = \text{Re}(-1) \rightarrow \text{Re}(z_1 - z_i) = 0$ , which forces that $z_i - z_i = 0$ for all $1 \le i \le n$ .
--------------**Claim.** $|P(x + 1) - P(x)| = 1$ *Proof.* Therefore, we know that $P(x) = (x - c)^n$ where $c$ is a root of $P(x)$ . Now, we know that $P(x)^2 - 1 = (P(x) - 1)(P(x) + 1)$ . Furthermore, notice that $\gcd(P(x) - 1, P(x) + 1) = 1$ . Thus, if $P(x + 1) = (x - c + 1)^n \mid P(x)^2 - 1$ , then either \[ P(x+ 1) \mid P(x) + 1 \ \text{or} \ P(x + 1) \mid P(x) - 1 \] However, $\text{deg} (P(x + 1)) = \text{deg} (P(x) + 1) = \text{deg} (P(x) - 1)$ , and the monic condition of $P(x)$ forces \[ P(x + 1) = P(x) + 1 \ \text{or} \ P(x + 1) = P(x) - 1 \] ------------------ At this point, it suffices to determine all polynomials of degree $n \ge 2$ such that $P(x + 1) = P(x) + 1$ or $P(x + 1) = P(x) - 1$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$ . (All these polynomials must satisfy the original equation). However, it's well known that all polynomials such that $P(x + 1) - P(x) = 1$ and $P(x + 1) - P(x) = -1$ are only linear polynomials.

stem_md: We are given a polyhedron with at least  $5$  vertices, such that exactly  $3$  edges meet in each of the vertices. Prove that we can assign a rational number to every vertex of the given polyhedron such that the following conditions are met: $(i)$  At least one of the numbers assigned to the vertices is equal to  $2020$ . $(ii)$  For every polygonal face, the product of the numbers assigned to the vertices of that face is equal to  $1$ .
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/AoPS Yearly Contest Collections/2020 Contests/2020 Serbian Mathematical Olympiad/2283427.json

candidates:
Let  $a=2020$ .
------**Case 1.** The polyhedron has a face  $F$  with an even number of vertices.
Place the numbers  $a$  and  $1/a$  alternately on the vertices of  $F$ , and put  $1$  on every other vertex of the polyhedron. Then the product of the numbers on the vertices of  $F$  is  $1$ . For any other face, it either has no common point with  $F$  (hence all its vertices contain  $1$  and the product is  $1$ ), or it contains an edge of  $F$  (whose two endpoints are labeled  $a$  and  $1/a$ , so the product is still  $1$ ). Thus, in this case the product over the vertices of every face equals  $1$ .
------**Case 2.** Every face of the polyhedron has an odd number of vertices.
Fix a vertex  $V$ . Let  $V_1,V_2,V_3$  be the three neighbors of  $V$  (connected to  $V$  via an edge). Let  $F_1$  be the face containing the edges  $VV_2$  and  $VV_3$ ; define  $F_2$  and  $F_3$  analogously using  $(VV_3,VV_1)$  and  $(VV_1,VV_2)$ , respectively. Since three noncollinear points determine a plane, we have that  $F_1$  and  $F_2$  have no common vertices other than  $V$  and  $V_3$ . Similar case for the pairs  $(F_2,F_3)$  and  $(F_3,F_1)$ .

Assign the number  $1$  to  $V,V_1,V_2,V_3$ . On the remaining vertices of  $F_1,F_2,F_3$  place the numbers  $a$  and  $1/a$  alternately, and do so in such a way that on the two edges  $V_iA$  and  $V_iB$  ( $A$  and  $B$  are vertices) incident to each  $V_i$  besides  $VV_i$ ,  $A$  and  $B$  receive different numbers (Note we can do this since  $F_1, F_2,F_3$  contain odd number of vertices). Then assign the value  $1$  to all the remaining vertices of the polyhedron.

Because a polyhedron has at least  $5$  vertices, the three faces  $F_1,F_2,F_3$  cannot all be triangles; hence at least one of  $F_1,F_2,F_3$  has a vertex carrying the label  $a$ .

With this assignment the product of the numbers on the vertices of each of  $F_1,F_2,F_3$  equals  $1$ . Moreover, any other face either has no common point with  $F_1,F_2,F_3$ , or contains an edge of one of  $F_1,F_2,F_3$ , or contains one of the two edges adjacent to some  $V_i$  (besides  $VV_i$ ). In all cases its vertex labels multiply to  $1$  as well.
------
Combining the two cases, the claim is proved.  $\Box$

stem_md: We are given a triangle  $ABC$ . Points  $D$  and  $E$  on the line  $AB$  are such that  $AD=AC$  and  $BE=BC$ , with the arrangment of points  $D - A - B - E$ . The circumscribed circles of the triangles  $DBC$  and  $EAC$  meet again at the point  $X\neq C$ , and the circumscribed circles of the triangles  $DEC$  and  $ABC$  meet again at the point  $Y\neq C$ . Find the measure of  $\angle ACB$  given the condition  $DY+EY=2XY$ .
solution_md:
WLOG  $CA\ge CB$ . $\textbf{Claim 1:}$   $X$  is the  $C$ -excenter of  $\triangle ABC$ . $\textit{Proof:}$  Define  $X'$  as the  $C$ -excenter. From easy angle chasing, we have  $\angle DCX'+\angle CX'A=90^{\circ} $  which implies  $X'A\perp CD$ . We also have  $CA=AD$ , hence  $X'A$  is the perpendicular bisector of  $CD$ . Therefore,
\[\angle X'DB=\angle X'DA=\angle X'CA=\angle X'CB\]
So,  $DCBX'$  is cyclic. Similarly, we can prove that  $ECAX'$  is cyclic. Therefore,  $X=X'$ .  $\textbf{Claim 2:}$   $X$  is the circumcenter of  $DCE$  $\textit{Proof:}$  Just note that as  $X$  is the  $C$ -excenter, we have  $XA$  is perpendicular bisector of  $CD$  and  $XB$  is perpendicular bisector of  $CE$ .

Now, define  $O$  as the circumcenter of  $ABC$  ,  $T$  as the midpoint of arc  $\widehat{AB}$  not containing  $C$  and  $Z$  as the reflection of  $X$  wrt line  $AB$ . By claim 2, we have  $XY=XC$ , hence  $XO$  is the perpendicular bisector of  $CY$ . $\textbf{Claim 3:}$   $T,Z,Y$  are collinear. $\textit{Proof:}$  Define  $F=ZT\cap AB$  and  $G$  such that  $GT$  is tangent to  $\odot (ABC)$  and  $A,G$  lies on the same side of  $CX$ . To prove the claim, we only need to prove that  $\angle ZTG=\angle YTG$ . Note that
\[\angle ZTG=\angle ZFA=90^{\circ}-\angle XZT\]
and we also have
\[\angle YTG=\angle YCT=\angle YCX=90^{\circ}-\angle OXC\]
So, we just need to prove that  $\angle XZT=\angle OXC$ . To do this, we will use complex number. As usual, we will use lowescript of a letter as it's complex coordinate. WLOG  $\odot (ABC)$  is a unit circle. Assign  $a=p^2, b=q^2,$  and  $c=r^2$ . Hence, we will have  $|p|=|q|=|r|=1$ . It's easy to check that  $t=-pq$  and  $x=qr+pr-pq$ . $Z$  is the reflection of  $X$  wrt to line  $AB$ , so
\[z=a+b-ab\overline{x}=p^2+q^2-p^2q^2(\frac{1}{qr}+\frac{1}{pr}-\frac{1}{pq})=\frac{p^2r+q^2r-p^2q-pq^2+pqr}{r}\]
It suffices to prove that  $\measuredangle CXO=\measuredangle XZT$  which equivalent to  $\frac{o-x}{c-x}: \frac{t-z}{x-z}\in \mathbb R$ . But we have
\[\frac{o-x}{c-x}:\frac{t-z}{x-z}=\frac{pq-pr-qr}{r^2-pr-qr+pq}\times \frac{qr+pr-pq-\frac{p^2r+q^2r-p^2q-pq^2+pqr}{r}}{-pq-\frac{p^2r+q^2r-p^2q-pq^2+pqr}{r}}=\frac{pq-pr-qr}{(r-p)(r-q)}\times \frac{\frac{(p+q)(r-p)(r-q)}{r}}{\frac{(p+q)(pq-pr-qr)}{r}}=1\]
Hence, the claim is true.

Define  $F=\overline{TZY}\cap AB$ . It's easy to see that we must have  $Y,Z$  lies on the same side of  $AB$ . Moreover, because  $T,Y\in \odot (ABC)$  and they are on different side of  $AB$ , we get that  $F$  must lie on segment  $AB$ . $\textbf{Claim 4:}$  The condition  $DY+EY=2XY$  implies  $Y=Z$  $\textit{Proof:}$  Notice that  $XY=XE=XD=ZE=ZD$ . So,  $DY+EY=2XY\implies DY+EY=DZ+EZ$ .
Assume the contrary that  $Y\neq Z$ . Then from  $F,Z,Y$  collinear,  $F$  lies on segment  $AB$ , and  $Y,Z$  lies on the same side of  $AB$ , we must have either  $Z$  lies strictly inside  $\triangle DYE$  or  $Y$  lies strictly inside  $\triangle DZE$ .
If  $Z$  lies strictly inside  $\triangle DYE$ , it's well known that  $DY+EY>DZ+EZ$ . A contradiction
Similarly, if  $Y$  lies strictly inside  $\triangle DZE$ , we have  $DZ+EZ>DY+EY$ . Again another contradiction
Therefore, we must have  $Y=Z$ . Claim 4 is now proven

Now notice that
\[\angle DYE=\angle DCE=\angle DCA+\angle ACB+\angle BCE=\frac{\angle CAB}{2}+\angle ACB+\frac{\angle CBA}{2}=90^{\circ}+\frac{\angle ACB}{2}\]
and we have
\[\angle DZE=\angle DXE=2(180^{\circ}-\angle DCE)=180^{\circ}-\angle ACB\]
Because  $Y=Z$ , then  $90^{\circ}+\frac{\angle ACB}{2}=180^{\circ}-\angle ACB\implies \angle ACB=\boxed{60^{\circ}}$ .

stem_md: In a trapezoid  $ABCD$  such that the internal angles are not equal to  $90^{\circ}$ , the diagonals  $AC$  and  $BD$  intersect at the point  $E$ . Let  $P$  and  $Q$  be the feet of the altitudes from  $A$  and  $B$  to the sides  $BC$  and  $AD$  respectively. Circumscribed circles of the triangles  $CEQ$  and  $DEP$  intersect at the point  $F\neq E$ . Prove that the lines  $AP$ ,  $BQ$  and  $EF$  are either parallel to each other, or they meet at exactly one point.
solution_md:
**Remark:** Through solution we assume that  $AB \parallel CD$ . If  $BC \parallel AD$ , then problem' s statement does not hold. 
Let  $CQ \cap PD =X$ . We begin with the following claim. **Claim:**  $X$  lies on  $EF$  **Proof:** Clearly  $ABPQ$  is cyclic quadrilateral. Note that:   $$  \angle BAQ = \angle CPQ \quad \text{and} \quad \angle CDQ = 180^{\circ} -\angle BAQ $$   
This implies that  $CDQP$  is cyclic. Now by radical axis theorem on  $\odot(CEQ)$ ,  $\odot(DEP)$  and  $\odot(CQDP)$  we have that  $X$  lies on  $EF$  as desired. 

Now by Pappus theorem on sets of points  $\{B,P,C\}$  and  $\{A,Q,D\}$  we have that  $AP \cap BQ$ ,  $E$ ,  $X$  are collinear. This actually implies that  $AP \cap BQ$  lies on  $EF$  as desired.

stem_md:
For a natural number  $n$ ,  with  $v_2(n)$  we denote the largest integer  $k\geq0$  such that  $2^k|n$ . Let us assume that the function  $f\colon\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$  meets the conditions: $(i)$   $f(x)\leq3x$  for all natural numbers  $x\in\mathbb{N}$ . $(ii)$   $v_2(f(x)+f(y))=v_2(x+y)$  for all natural numbers  $x,y\in\mathbb{N}$ .

Prove that for every natural number  $a$  there exists exactly one natural number  $x$  such that  $f(x)=3a$ .
solution_md:
Super painful problem, took over 8 hours of value-grinding (which are absolutely extraneous, explained in Motivation). Also probably same as post $\#5$ (I solved this slower, when I worked on this problem with @IndoMath) but posting anyways because this problem is very cool. Denote the usual assertion of plugging in $(x,y)$ in the second condition by $P(x,y)$ . $\color{green} \rule{25cm}{3pt}$ $\textcolor{green}{\textbf{\text{Easy observation.}}}$ If we have proven that $\{6\cdot \mathbb{N}_{0}+3 \} \in$ range $f(2 \cdot \mathbb{N}_{0}+1)$ we are done. $\textcolor{green}{\textbf{\text{Proof 0.}}}$ First, by $P(x,x)$ we have \[ v_2(2f(x)) = v_2(2x) \] which implies $\{\text{odd} \}$ maps to $\{\text{odd} \}$ , $\{ 2 \pmod 4\}$ maps to $\{ 2 \pmod 4 \}$ , $\ldots$ Also, observe that the domain of $f$ can be safely grouped (a.k.a. put into bubbles of their own) according to their $v_2$ s; for example, a substitution in form of $P(2 \pmod 4, 4 \pmod 8)$ yields \[ v_2(2 \ (\text{mod} \ 4)) = v_2(2\ (\text{mod} \ 4)) \] which absolutely means nothing. Having said so, the assertion $P(x,y)$ holds value iff $v_2(x) = v_2(y)$ , and so if one succesfully proves that $f(\text{odd})$ 's range contains all odd multiples of $3$ $\textbf{using only the assertion when x,y odd}$ , then analogously one has proven that $f( 2 \pmod 4)$ also contains all $"2 \pmod 4"$ s which are multiples of $3$ $\textbf{using only the assertion when x,y 2 mod 4}$ , and so on. $\color{green} \rule{25cm}{0.5pt}$ $\textcolor{cyan}{\textbf{\text{Heuristic on which all calculations are based.}}}$ If $x+y = 2^k$ for some $k$ , and $f(x) \ne 3x$ or $f(x) \ne 3y$ , then \[ f(x) + f(y) = 2^k \] $\textcolor{cyan}{\textbf{\text{Proof 1.}}}$ By $P(x,y)$ we get that \[v_2(f(x)+f(y)) = k\] which altogether with $f(x) + f(y) \leq 3x + 3y$ implies $f(x)+f(y) = 2^k$ or $3 \cdot 2^k$ . If either of $f(x)$ or $f(y)$ does not attain its maximum at $3x$ or $3y$ , then equality of $f(x)+f(y)$ at $3 \cdot 2^k$ cannot be attained, therefore the first option must hold. $\blacksquare$ $\color{cyan} \rule{25cm}{0.1pt}$ $\textcolor{blue}{\textbf{\text{Regularity of range up to a certain threshold.}}}$ Putting the cutoff at $2^k$ , we can be certain that $f(x \leq 2^k)$ (which has $2^{k-1}$ terms) is injective $\pmod{{2}^{k}}$ ; therefore also surjective (for all odd residue classes, of course). $\textcolor{blue}{\textbf{\text{Proof 2.}}}$ If $f(x) \equiv f(y) \pmod{{2}^{k}}$ , then (even without using the $\textcolor{cyan}{\textbf{\text{Heuristic}}}$ ) we get \[f(2^k-y) \equiv -f(y) \pmod{{2}^{k}} \] by $P(y,2^k-y)$ . However, $P(x,2^k-y)$ implies \[ v_2(f(x)+f(2^k-y)) < k \] as $x+2^k-y \ne 2^k$ , while also being less than $2^{k+1}$ (therefore must be of lower power). A contradiction. $\blacksquare$ $\color{magenta} \rule{25cm}{4pt}$ $\textcolor{magenta}{\textbf{\text{Additive inverses of 3x + putting it together with size.}}}$ Let the magic happen! We now finish the proof. Let $3x \notin$ range. Consider the threshold $2^k < 3x < 2^{k+1}$ , and consider the classes of $f$ from $f(1),f(3),\ldots, f(2^k-1)$ . Now let $f(a) \equiv 2^{k+1}-3x \pmod{2^k}$ . [color = purple]**Case 1.**[/color] $f(a) = 2^{k+1}-3x$ . Then, since $f(a) \ne 0 \pmod 3$ , $\mathbf{f(a) \ne 3a}$ (Magic spell no.1: Obvious but tricky to find.) Then, by $\textcolor{cyan}{\textbf{\text{Heuristic}}}$ , $f(2^{k+1}-a) = 2^{k+1} - (2^{k+1}-3x) = 3x.$ [color = purple]**Case 2.**[/color] $f(a) \ne 2^{k+1} - 3x$ . Then, since by $\textcolor{blue}{\textbf{\text{Regularity}}}$ (or by the sentence before **Case 1**), $f(a) \equiv 2^{k+1}-3x \pmod{2^k}$ . However, that implies $f(a) \in \{2^{k} + 2^{k+1}-3x, 2^{k}+2^{k}+2^{k+1}-3x\} $ since $f(a) \leq 3a \leq 3\cdot 2^k$ . However, we do not use this choice up to its full potential; we only use that $f(a) > 2^k$ (Magic Spell no.2: Why must we ignore the juicy and definite details of $"$ two possible images $"$ for an indefinite size argument?). Again, by $\textcolor{cyan}{\textbf{\text{Heuristic}}}$ , since $f(a) + f(2^k-a) > f(a) > 2^k$ , so we must have $f(a) = 3a$ and \[f(2^k-a) = 3(2^k-a) = 3(2^k - (2^k-x)) = 3x,\] since out of $\{2^{k} + 2^{k+1}-3x, 2^{k}+2^{k}+2^{k+1}-3x\}$ , the perfect fit for $3a$ , which is a multiple of $3$ , is only the first option (which implies $a =2^k-x $ ). We are done. $\blacksquare$ $\blacksquare$ $\blacksquare$
Motivation: ALL the pitfalls of considering structures outside range --- and why the magic is as it is.Immediately after I started I knew this was going to be a ride of the year --- they didn't give me anything to work for, literally! No standard Cauchy, no direct surjectivity (injectivity is laughably easy to proof, which I directly discarded since it didn't bear any weight), no consideration for any prime outside $2$ , and a condition absurdly difficult to visualize (who would ever ask why $3a$ is in the range of a $v_2$ function?) After noting that only $(odd,odd)$ should be considered, as $(odd,even)$ is useless and $(even,even)$ is just a $"$ dilation $"$ of $f$ by 2, unfortunately, most of my 5 first hours only misled me further and further. \[\begin{tabular}{p{12cm}} $\rule{4cm}{0.5pt} \hspace{1cm} \bigstar \hspace{1cm} \rule{4cm}{0.5pt}$ \end{tabular} \]**S1 (5 points). Soft Tech 0 and 1 (Odd elimination, trying small cases)**At the time, I thought that if $f(1) = 1$ , it is easily proven that $f(n) = n$ . As I breathed my first sigh of relief, I was quickly faced with the bizarre case of $f(1) = 3$ , as one of these will happen: \[ \begin{tabular}{cc|cc} $f(3)=1$ & $f(5)=7$ & $f(3)=1$ & $f(5) = 7$ $f(7)=5$ & $f(9)=11$ & $f(7)=21$ & $f(9)=27$ \hline $f(3)=9$ & $f(5)=15$ & $f(3)=9$ & $f(5) = 15$ $f(7)=5$ & $f(9)=11$ & $f(7)=21$ & $f(9)=27$ \end{tabular} \] When $f(k) = 3k$ for $k = \{3,5,7,9\}$ or $3 \rightarrow 5$ , $5 \rightarrow 3, 7 \rightarrow 9, 9 \rightarrow 7$ it is easy to induct to infinity. $\textcolor{green}{\text{Section 1 End.}}$ \[\begin{tabular}{p{12cm}} $\rule{4cm}{0.5pt} \hspace{1cm} \bigstar \bigstar \bigstar \hspace{1cm} \rule{4cm}{0.5pt}$ \end{tabular} \]**S2 (15 points). Hard Tech 1 (Bash for monsters): took up a lot of hours to "convince myself wrongly" that periodicity matters.** But the two remaining cases makes all the weird functions to the equation. When we continue the second option, we get \[ \begin{tabular}{c|c} \hline $11$ & $\{9\}$ \hline $13$ & $\{15\}$ \hline $15$ & $\{13,45\}$ \hline $17$ & $\{19,51\}$ \hline $19$ & $\{17\}$ \hline $21$ & $\{23\}$ \hline $23$ & $\{5,69\}$ \hline $25$ & $\{11,75\}$ \hline \end{tabular} \] however, this became more chaotic the lower we go; on $f(15)$ and $f(17)$ there are only two choices of $13,19$ or $45,51$ , but on the lower ones there are already "four options": $f(23)$ can really be $5$ or $69$ without too much concern, and so does $f(25)$ . This also led me to my first monster, which is this function $\textbf{in its best case!} $ of $f(8k+3) = 8k+1, f(8k+5) = 8k+7, f(8k+7) = 24k+21, f(8k+1) = 24k+3.$ This got even more $"$ chaotic $"$ in the third choice: \[ \begin{tabular}{c|c|c} \hline $x$ &\text{possible results}& $f(x)$ \hline $3$ && $9$ \hline $5$ && $15$ \hline $7$ & $21-16$ & $5$ \hline $9$ & $27-16$ & $11$ \hline $11$ & $33\ominus32$ &\{33,\textcolor{blue}{1}\} \hline $13$ & $39\ominus32$ &\{\textcolor{red}{39},7\} \hline $15$ & $45\ominus32$ & \hline $17$ & $51\ominus32$ & \hline $19$ & $57\ominus32$ &\{\textcolor{red}{57},25\} \hline $21$ & $63\ominus32$ &\{63,\textcolor{blue}{31}\} \hline $23$ & $69-48$ & $21$ \hline $25$ & $75-48$ & $27$ \hline $27$ & $81\ominus64$ &\{81,17\} \hline \end{tabular} \] where no patterns seem to show itself clearly. (Here $a \ominus b = \{a,a-b\} = (a+0) \cup (a-b)$ ) The only "nice" thing that I saw was that when $f(11)$ is $1$ , $f(21)$ is uniquely determined (as shown by the purple color) and so does $13,19$ . Worse still, $15$ and $17$ are $"$ undetermined $"$ (like in the previous case), and the difference in possible values can be $32, 48 $ or $64$ . Continuing this I get my second monster function (which fortunately brought me back to the correct path, but also straying me again later); seeing that we can fix the first 16 values and assume the rest is periodic: \[ \begin{tabular}{ccccccccc} $x$ & $16k+1$ & $16k+3$ & $16k+5$ & $16k+7$ & $16k+9$ & $16k+11$ & $16k+13$ & $16k+15$ \hline $f(x)$ & $16k+3$ & $48k+19$ & $16k+15$ & $16k+5$ & $16k+11$ & $16k+14$ & $48k+39$ & $16k+13$ \end{tabular} \] which to my dismay, actually works. Then, all my initial arguments of hoping to divide all numbers into groups of either $8,16$ or such directly fails because of the $\textbf{fractal-like}$ nature of these functions; also all direct and naive 'classical' bounding such as $f(x) \equiv 3x \pmod{2^k}$ will not work, as we can have $f(x) = 3x-48$ for some $x$ , while also being $f(x) = x\pm 10$ for some other $x$ in the second monster. $\textcolor{green}{\text{Section 2 End. }}$ \[\begin{tabular}{p{12cm}} $\rule{4cm}{0.5pt} \hspace{1cm} \bigstar \hspace{1cm} \rule{4cm}{0.5pt}$ \end{tabular} \]**S3 (5 points). Soft Tech 2 (Inequality utilization?): Where do I put the first condition to maximize my gains?** I had already lost the point of the problem by this point, so I reexamined the statement and noticed I hadn't even tried to put the inequality to its rightful place, which is ... $\textbf{inside the v-2 brackets!}$ and so I just blankly stared at the inequality $f(x) + f(y) \leq 3x+3y$ ; and if $x+y$ has a lot of non- $2$ primes the equality is mostly useless --- the only times when it's strong and actually delimiting is when $x+y = 2^k$ . Then came the first $\textcolor{cyan}{\textbf{\text{Heuristic}}}$ . $\textcolor{green}{\text{Section 3 End.}}$ \[\begin{tabular}{p{12cm}} $\rule{4cm}{0.5pt} \hspace{1cm} \bigstar \hspace{1cm} \rule{4cm}{0.5pt}$ \end{tabular} \]**S4 (5 points). Hard Tech 2 (FE, Range detection): noticing the complete nature of the functions using mod 16 mindset.**Back to the objectives, I wondered how one could show that $3a$ must exist in such monster. Then, I realized that a number which does not show up on the $16k+a$ of the range's sides, must indeed be packed in the $48k+19$ and $48k+39$ . When expanding the range of the first $16$ numbers, which is \[ \{3,9,15,5,11,1,39,13,19,57,31,21,27,17,87,29\}\] which contains $\textbf{all numbers until 32}$ except $\textbf{arguably \{7,9,23,25\}}$ , with the addition of 'high' multiples of $3$ : $9,39,57,87$ , which are of $\textbf{7,9,23,25}$ mod $32$ ! There came the idea to use injectivity on mods, as the 'missing numbers' is just actually replaced with bigger numbers which (must be) multiples of $3$ ! My journey is half over, after I identified that the $\textcolor{cyan}{\textbf{\text{Heuristic}}}$ makes sure that the range of first $16$ numbers which are not high must be less than $32$ , and once a high number, such as $39$ is seen on the range, not only does it makes us sure that it's a multiple of $3$ ; but it also ensures us that we have captured $f(13)$ which must be $39$ and also ensures the value of $f(19)$ . $\textcolor{green}{\text{Section 4 End.}}$ \[\begin{tabular}{p{12cm}} $\rule{4cm}{0.5pt} \hspace{1cm} \hspace{1cm} \rule{4cm}{0.5pt}$ \end{tabular} \]**S5. Slowly letting go of the periodicity, and switching to "large range"s that can occur after 32.**Then here, once again I fell into madness. While I had quite the right mindset of proving that, say, $33$ 's preimage must be in $[33,64]$ if not already visible as a 'high number' in the prior range, I was too focused on the $\textit{golden pairs}$ of $f(a) = 3a$ . This is because it seems that once a pair, say, $(3,29)$ must form $(9,87)$ --- we know by $\textcolor{cyan}{\textbf{\text{Heuristic}}}$ that $f(13)$ and $f(19)$ are ensured. However, there's a problem with the opposite direction, which I noticed only later. If $f(13) = 39$ , then as $39 > 32$ we can be sure that $19$ is also $"$ golden $"$ , but $f(3) = 9$ does not imply $f(29) = 87$ . For a more concrete example: \[ \begin{tabular}{c|c} $1\rightarrow3$ & $17\rightarrow19$ $3\rightarrow9$ & $19\rightarrow57$ $5\rightarrow15$ & $21\rightarrow31$ $7\rightarrow5$ & $23\rightarrow21$ $9\rightarrow11$ & $25\rightarrow27$ $11\rightarrow\textcolor{cyan}{\textbf{1}}$ & $27\rightarrow\textcolor{red}{\textbf{17}}$ $13\rightarrow39$ & $29\rightarrow87$ $15\rightarrow13$ & $31\rightarrow29$ \end{tabular} \text{into} \begin{tabular}{c|c} $1\rightarrow3$ & $17\rightarrow19$ $3\rightarrow9$ & $19\rightarrow57$ $5\rightarrow15$ & $21\rightarrow31$ $7\rightarrow5$ & $23\rightarrow21$ $9\rightarrow11$ & $25\rightarrow27$ $11\rightarrow\textcolor{cyan}{\textbf{1}}$ & $27\rightarrow\textcolor{red}{\textbf{81}}$ $13\rightarrow39$ & $29\rightarrow87$ $15\rightarrow13$ & $31\rightarrow29$ \end{tabular} \] where $f(5) + f(11)$ may as well be $16$ but $f(5)+f(27)$ can be large for its size (a.k.a $96 = 3 \cdot 32$ ). Before this, my initial plan was to differentiate $"$ nice things $"$ of $f(x) = 3x$ and $"$ fallen things $"$ such as the case with $f(5) = 15$ and $f(11) = 1$ , but I realized that these two may intersect more than I expected. $\textcolor{green}{\text{Section 5 End.}}$ \[\begin{tabular}{p{12cm}} $\rule{4cm}{0.5pt} \hspace{1cm} \text{0.5}\bigstar \hspace{1cm} \rule{4cm}{0.5pt}$ \end{tabular} \]**S6 (2.5 points). Hard Tech 3 (FE): finding out the missing numbers and where to fill the large multiples of 3 could've been in the range.**I was sighing heavily because looking at the $\textcolor{blue}{\textbf{\text{Regularity of range up to 32}}}$ yields mixed results --- initially after getting that, I planned to prove the existence of, say, $f(x) = 33$ by looking at the places $1$ or $17$ must appear, and then add that with $16$ somehow to later get $33$ in $f(43)$ or something. Here I realized I had not utilized the full power and promise of the $\textcolor{cyan}{\textbf{\text{Heuristic}}}$ --- which is: when $f(x) > 32$ , then this blows up many possibilities. Rather looking at gloomy places such as $f(5) = 15$ , where anomalies to the $\textcolor{cyan}{\textbf{\text{Heuristic}}}$ happens a lot, I looked at $f(13)$ which has nice values. As $39 \equiv 7 \pmod{32}$ , I tried to 'prove', say $f(x) = 57$ --- which the $\textcolor{cyan}{\textbf{\text{Heuristic}}}$ successfully utilized in its full power (There comes Magic Spell 1.) $\textcolor{green}{\text{Section 6; a.k.a. magic spell 1; End.}}$ \[\begin{tabular}{p{12cm}} $\rule{4cm}{0.5pt} \hspace{1cm} \bigstar \hspace{1cm} \rule{4cm}{0.5pt}$ \end{tabular} \]**S7 (5 points). Soft Tech 3 (Being conscientious on the Heuristic): Seeing it at a deeper level of "what does it say for non-multiples of 3"?**Then, surprise, surprise! If the existence of the class $39 \pmod{32}$ isn't 'golden' like above, it must be $f(x) = 7$ which is small; but $\textbf{fortunately not a multiple of 3!}$ I hesitated to look at these 'ugly' non-multiples-of- $3$ before, but after I tried to prove the existence of $f^{-1}(51)$ , and even $f^{-1}(33)$ in this way (by looking at range classes of $13 \pmod{32}, 31 \pmod{32}$ ) that the resulting classes uncannily ensures that when $\textbf{large numbers pop up, they're a multiple of 3}$ and when $\textbf{small numbers pop up, they must not be a multiple of 3.}$ Then this is realized in the second magic spell, where, of course, $2^{k+1} - 3x$ is not a multiple of $3$ , which directly yields the desired conclusion. $\textcolor{green}{\text{ Motivation End.}}$ \[\begin{tabular}{p{12cm}} $\rule{4cm}{0.5pt} \hspace{1cm} \blacksquare \hspace{1cm} \rule{4cm}{0.5pt}$ \end{tabular} \]**Final comments.** Still, if you're still reading this long-winding exposition, then thanks a lot! From what I see, this manipulation of $v_2$ thing has been popping recently (2012 A7, I'm pointing fingers at you!) and they also have lots of traps if you flip signs (minus to plus --- had I considered $64-33$ earlier rather than $33-32$ ) or flip directions (looking at ranges vs looking at good $"\textit{golden pairs}"$ ) without rethinking what it is you're trying to prove. It really looks short and sweet, but unless you have the right mindset, this can really screw you over with the $64$ -class monsters that have high variability while also is uncannily categorizable using cleverly-designed $\textbf{Claims.}$ Total: 37.5 points --- I would rate this 35-40M in terms of MOHS.

For a natural number $n$ , with $v_2(n)$ we denote the largest integer $k\geq0$ such that $2^k|n$ . Let us assume that the function $f\colon\mathbb{N} o\mathbb{N}$ meets the conditions: $(i)$ $f(x)\leq3x$ for all natural numbers $x\in\mathbb{N}$ . $(ii)$ $v_2(f(x)+f(y))=v_2(x+y)$ for all natural numbers $x,y\in\mathbb{N}$ . Prove that for every natural number $a$ there exists exactly one natural number $x$ such that $f(x)=3a$ .
Really hard problem. :( :( Let $P(x,y)$ be the assertion of $x$ and $y$ to the given functional condition: \[ u_2(f(x) + f(y)) = u_2(x + y) \] If there exists two distinct natural numbers $m$ and $n$ such that $f(m) = f(n) = 3a$ , then consider a natural number $y$ such that $ u_2(y+m) ot= u_2(y+n)$ . If such number doesn't exists, then $m \equiv n \ ( ext{mod}\ 2^k)$ for all large $k$ , forcing $m = n$ , a contradiction. But we then have \[ u_2(y+m) = u_2(f(y) + f(m)) = u_2(f(y) + f(n)) = u_2(y+n) \] which is a contradiction. ----------- We just need to prove that there exists a preimage of $3a$ for every $a \in \mathbb{N}$ . Note that from $P(x,x)$ , we have $ u_2(f(x)) = u_2(x)$ for every $x$ .
Note.Now, notice that $P(x,y)$ won't give useful information unless $ u_2(x) = u_2(y)$ . This is because if WLOG $ u_2(x) > u_2(y)$ , then $ u_2(f(x)) > u_2(f(y))$ , which means that \[ u_2(f(x) + f(y)) = u_2(f(y)) = u_2(y) = u_2(x + y) \]
**Claim.** For any odd numbers $x$ and $y$ such that $x + y = 2^k$ , then $f(x) + f(y) = 2^k$ or $f(x) = 3x$ and $f(y) = 3y$ simultaneously. *Proof.* To prove the statement, we consider $ u_2(a)$ . Now, consider all numbers $n$ from set $\mathcal{N} = \{ n \mid u_2(n) = u_2(a) \}$ . We want to find an $n$ such that $f(n) = 3a$ . \[ u_2(x + y) = u_2(f(x) + f(y)) \] Take $y = 2^A - x$ for values $A > u_2(x)$ for a fixed $x$ , it is immediate to check that $ u_2(x) = u_2(y)$ . This would forces $$ f(y) \equiv -f(x) + 2^A \ ( ext{mod} \ 2^{A + 1}) $$ This forces $f(y) = 2^A - f(x)$ or $f(y) = 3 \cdot 2^A - f(x)$ for all $A > u_2(x)$ , or otherwise, $2 \cdot 2^{A + 1} + 2^A - f(x) > 3 \cdot (2^A - f(x))$ , contradiction to the first condition. We basically conclude that for any number $a \in \mathcal{N}$ and $A > u_2(a)$ and $2^A > a$ , then \[ f(2^A - a) = 2^A - f(a) \ ext{or} \ f(2^A - a) = 3 \cdot 2^A - f(a) \] and by **Remark** where $\mathcal{N}_k$ is defined as $\{ n \mid n \in \mathbb{N} , u_2(n) = k \}$ , we can simplify the condition into dealing with just odd numbers instead. ---------**Claim. (Injectivity in mod $2^k$ )** We have $x ot \equiv y \ ( ext{mod} \ 2^k)$ if and only if $f(x) ot \equiv f(y) \ ( ext{mod} \ 2^k)$ . *Proof.* Suppose otherwise, that there exists $x ot \equiv y \ ( ext{mod} \ 2^k)$ but $f(x) \equiv f(y) \ ( ext{mod} \ 2^k)$ . The other direction is dealt similarly. -------------- Now, let $k$ be an integer such that $2^{k - 1} < 3a < 2^k$ . Consider \[ f(1), f(3), \dots, f(2^k - 1) \] Now, take odd values $1 \le x \le 2^k - 1$ such that $f(x) \equiv 3a \ ( ext{mod} \ 2^k)$ . This must exists since $f(1), f(3), \dots, f(2^k - 1)$ take on only odd values modulo $2^k$ and by injectivity, this implies surjectivity. Now, suppose that $f(x) ot= 3a$ , then we have \[ 2^k \le | f(x) - 3a | \] If $f(x) < 2^k$ , then we have $|f(x) - 3a| \le \max \{ f(x) - 3a, 3a - f(x) \} \le \max \{ 2^k - 3a, 2^k - f(x) \} < 2^k$ , which is a contradiction. stem_md: We are given a natural number  $k$ . Let us consider the following game on an infinite onedimensional board. At the start of the game, we distrubute  $n$  coins on the fields of the given board (one field can have multiple coins on itself). After that, we have two choices for the following moves: $(i)$  We choose two nonempty fields next to each other, and we transfer all the coins from one of the fields to the other. $(ii)$  We choose a field with at least  $2$  coins on it, and we transfer one coin from the chosen field to the  $k-\mathrm{th}$  field on the left , and one coin from the chosen field to the  $k-\mathrm{th}$  field on the right. $\mathbf{(a)}$  If  $n\leq k+1$ , prove that we can play only finitely many moves. $\mathbf{(b)}$  For which values of  $k$  we can choose a natural number  $n$  and distribute  $n$  coins on the given board such that we can play infinitely many moves.
solution_md:
Painful problem. The places where combinatorics brings you ... 
Call the first move by  $(p_m,c_m,L)$  or  $(p_m,c_m,R)$  if the  $c_m$  coins move from the  $p_m^{th}$  position left-wise or right-wise. Call the second move  $(p_m,D)$  if two coins from the  $p_m^{th}$  position are distributed, one left by  $k$  positions and the other right by  $k$  positions.  $\color{blue} \rule{25cm}{1.5pt}$  $\color{blue} \textbf{\text{Part a.}}$  Separate the entire one-dimensional board into  $k$  classes modulo  $k$ . Notice that once a cell is empty forever, the board is (almost) effectively divided into two regions: on the left side of that cell and on the right side of that cell --- and no move  $(p_m,v_m,L/R)$  can be operated betwen the two regions. 

Now, if some modulo  $k$  class is empty at some point, it's easy to prove that they will be empty forever. If so, note that with finitely many coins, only finite amounts of the second operation will be done before the first operation must commence. When letting  $x_l$  be the amount of coins in the  $k-1$  cells of the  $l^{th}$  block ( $l$  can be negative, whenever we deem it so), the game is now equivalent to the second operation with  $k$  equal to  $1$ . This can be proven (later) that the game will end. 

If no class can be empty at any point, one class must have 2 coins, and the others must have 1 coin. From this state, either the two coins in one class gets operated by the second operation, or one coin gets transferred by the first operation. These two operations must be performed alternatingly, for one cannot perform the first move twice or a cell with 3 coins will appear, and one cannot perform the second move twice or he would get 2 classes with 2 coins or one class with 3 coins beforehand. 

And, more observations can be made! Since any two consecutive operations must take place using cells of that value (for example:  $(2,D)$ , then  $(k+2,1,L)$ , then  $(k+1,D)$ , then  $(1,1,L)$ ,  $\ldots$ ) we can set one coin to  $\textbf{always be moving}$ ; i.e. we can paint it green. That green coin must visit all other coins during the game, or else one coin will never be used and we might as well remove it. 

Consider the position of the leftmost coin. It cannot be bounded, because if it is then when that coin is visited by the green coin, they both must move right. Then, the range (i.e. the distance between the leftmost and rightmost coin) of the game must be unbounded, and by PHP we will get a gap with length  $\geq k+2$ . Then, the green coin will be stuck at the left portion or the right portion of the gap for the rest of the game, rendering the coins on the other portion of the one-dimensional grid useless.  $\blacksquare$   $\color{yellow} \rule{25cm}{1pt}$  $\color{yellow} \textbf{\text{Lemma.}}$  We play the game with the same one-dimensional board, however  $k$  is set to  $1$  and move (i) does not exist. Then the game will end in finitely many moves.  $\color{yellow} \textbf{\text{Proof of the Lemma.}}$  Again we follow the idea of 1994 C5, we will fix a coin on a transfer point.  To be rigorous, define a transfer point  $t$  to be the link between position  $t$  and  $t+1$ . We say a coin to belong in  $t$  if that coin was the first one to move between that link --- and then whenever that coin must be passed, it stays either in position  $t$  or  $t+1$ . 

Define the value of a coin in the cells be  $\ldots, 8, 4, 2, 1, 2, 4, 8,\ldots$ , and the value of a certain position in-game be the total value of its coins. If the game has infinitely many turns, with each turn increasing the total value, the total value will be unbounded. 

We consider two cases. If at some point all of the coins belong to some transfer point, the total value will be bounded; it is at most  $n\cdot 2^x$  where  $x$  is equal to  $\max$ (|rightmost transfer point|, |leftmost transfer point|). If at no point all the coins belong to some transfer point, then its value will also be bounded by the transfer points of the coins already belonging to some transfer point. Contradiction.  $\blacksquare$   $\color{magenta} \rule{25cm}{3pt}$  $\color{magenta} \textbf{\text{Part b.}}$  All  $k$ . This is possible using only  $5k$  coins. We will construct a periodic game (for  $k = 4$ , where higher  $k$  are analogous), implying it to last for infinitely many turns. 
Set the start position to be
\[ 1111 \quad 1111 \quad 1111 \quad 1111 \quad 1111\]
with the leftmost cell to be in position  $1$  (and the rightmost =  $20$ )
Now perform  $(1,1,R), (2,2,R), (3,3,R)$  and  $(4,4,R)$ , then  $(5,D), (5,3,R), (6,D), (6,2,R), (7,D), (7,1,R)$  and finally  $(8,D)$ . Do the same for the right side reversed, to yield
\[ 1111 \quad 0000 \quad 3333 \quad 0000 \quad 1111 \]
and we can finish with  $(9,D), (10,D), (11,D)$  and  $(12,D)$ .  $\blacksquare$   $\blacksquare$   $\blacksquare$ <details><summary>Section overview, final rating</summary>**[color = blue] Section 1: 5 points. [/color]** Soft Tech (Game observation): Stack formation and deformation.

Final Comments: What I missed this whole time was that in order for a particular game to be bounded; i.e. the coins won't move to infinity, is that there needs to be two positions in the game to have an equal number of coins. Indeed, infinite PHP guarantees this --- and this is also the simplest way to show that a game never ends, typically on a finitely dimensioned game (some games has unclear amount of dimensions, when it's hard to specify positions only by their  $\textit{raw positions}$ .) Most of the time, when proving that a game never end, there needs to be a clever monovariant setting like in (a); it's certainly a big leap to assume (after lots of hard work in the first part) that for big amounts of  $k$ , the game can still go.
