stem_md:
Let  $p$  be an odd prime, and put  $N=\frac{1}{4} (p^3 -p) -1.$  The numbers  $1,2, \dots, N$  are painted arbitrarily in two colors, red and blue. For any positive integer  $n \leqslant N,$  denote  $r(n)$  the fraction of integers  $\{ 1,2, \dots, n \}$  that are red.
Prove that there exists a positive integer  $a \in \{ 1,2, \dots, p-1\}$  such that  $r(n) \neq a/p$  for all  $n = 1,2, \dots , N.$ *Netherlands*
solution_md:
To my initial surprise, this is actually an (almost) pure C problem. As explained in the later part of the Solution, the things that can  $\textbf{actually swing}$  the average lies at the front of the pack, and no adjustment can be made for the  $a/p$  that has yet to be covered. 

--------
Note that  $r(n) = \dfrac{a}{p}$  only if  $n = kp$  for some  $k \in \mathbb{N}$ . Following that, naturally call a sequence of numbers  $(k-1)p+1,(k-1)p+2,\ldots,kp$  as the  $k^{\text{th}}$   $\color{green} \textbf{\textit{block}}$ . 

To alleviate the pesky appearance of the phrase  $r(n)$ , we assign the number placeholder  $r_1,r_2,\ldots,r_{p-1}$  so that  $r(r_ap) = \dfrac{a}{p}$ . This is equivalent to saying that each number  $a \in \{1,2,\ldots,p-1\}$  is satisfied at the end of the  $r_a^{\text{th}}$  block.  $\color{green} \rule{6cm}{2pt}$   $\color{green} \diamondsuit$   $ \boxed{\textbf{The Order of the Extremes.}}$   $\color{green} \diamondsuit$   $\color{green} \rule{6cm}{2pt}$  
Let there exists a good arrangement so that the numbers  $r_1$  until  $r_{p-1}$  exist. Now, we can WLOG that  $p-1$  appears first; i.e.  $r_{p-1} < r_1$ . 

This is because we can flip all switches, so all reds become blues and vice versa. This will cause the old config's  $r(kp) = \dfrac{a}{p}$  to change to  $r(kp) = \dfrac{p-a}{p}$ , so  $r_1$  and  $r_{p-1}$ 's position will switch with one another. 

Now, since  $r_1$  comes last, let the numbers  $r_{p-1}, r_{p-2}, \ldots,r_a$  already come before  $r_1$ 's existence, with  $a$  the lowest number which satisfies that statement.  $\color{green} \rule{25cm}{0.3pt}$   $\color{red} \rule{8.65cm}{2pt}$   $\color{red} \clubsuit$   $\color{red} \boxed{\textbf{One Member from the Full-House Missing.}}$   $\color{red} \clubsuit$   $\color{red} \rule{8.65cm}{2pt}$  
We claim that  $a \geq \dfrac{p+3}{2}$ . In other words, the house of big averages 
\[ r_{\frac{p+1}{2}}, r_{\frac{p+3}{2}}, \ldots, r_{p-2}, r_{p-1} \]
won't be flooding the grid before the extreme small average  $r_1$  comes along.  $\color{green} \rule{25cm}{0.3pt}$   $\color{magenta} \blacksquare$   $\color{magenta} \text{(after conjuring the extremal, you're pretty much almost a third of the way.)}$ -------- $\color{red} \spadesuit$   $\color{red} \boxed{\textbf{Proof.}}$   $\color{red} \spadesuit$  
Now let  $a \leq \dfrac{p+1}{2}$ . This means that all  $r_{\frac{p+1}{2}}$  up to the largest average  $r_{p-1}$  has appeared (and we do not consider the averages from the smaller house  $r_{\frac{p-1}{2}}$  or below.) 

Continuing the trend of considering the  $\textsf{latest}$ , consider the largest out of  $r_{\frac{p+1}{2}}$  to  $r_{p-1}$ . That number, say it is  $r_b$ , must satisfy 
\[ r_b \geq \dfrac{p-1}{2}\] 
as all the numbers  $r_i$ ,  $\dfrac{p+1}{2} \leq i \leq p-1, i \ne b$  has appeared before him. 

So, there has existed  $br_b \geq \dfrac{p-1}{2} \cdot b \geq \dfrac{p^2-1}{4}$  reds before  $r_1$ . This directly yields a contradiction, as we only have  $\dfrac{p^2-1}{4}-1$  blocks available; meaning that the number of reds before  $r_1$  must be less than  $\dfrac{p^2-1}{4}$ .  $\blacksquare$   $\blacksquare$  

-------- $\color{red} \rule{8.5cm}{2pt}$   $\color{red} \clubsuit$   $\color{red} \boxed{\textbf{As the Member comes, the Party is Over.}}$   $\color{red} \clubsuit$   $\color{red} \rule{8.5cm}{2pt}$  
We claim that after  $r_{p-1}$  up to  $r_a$  appears before  $r_1$ ,  $r_{a-1}$  cannot fit in due to the overflow of blue numbers. 

Note: we can be sure that  $r_{a-1}$  cannot  $\textit{sneak in}$  to the party before  $r_1$  due to the minimality assumption at the end of  $\color{green} \diamondsuit$   $ \boxed{\textbf{The Order of the Extremes}}$   $\color{green} \diamondsuit$ .  $\color{red} \rule{25cm}{0.3pt}$   $\color{red} \spadesuit$   $\color{red} \boxed{\textbf{Proof.}}$   $\color{red} \spadesuit$  
This is also easily explained. Since we already have at least  $(p-a)a$  red points before the end of the  $r_1^{\text{th}}$ , so we can be certain that at the end of the  $r_1^{\text{th}} \geq (p-a)a^{\text{th}}$  block, there exists a proportionate number of reds. 

We will similarly prove that the existing blue points after the  $r_1^{\text{th}}$  block,  $(p-1)(p-a)a$ , cannot warrant the existence of  $r_{a-1}$  which requires a relatively large red-density  $\left( \dfrac{a-1}{p}\right)$  of points before it. 

Since there are only less than  $\dfrac{p^2-1}{4}$  blocks, the total number of blues that exist  $\textbf{before}$  the  $r_{a-1}^{\text{th}}$  block is less than  $\dfrac{p^2-1}{4}(p-a+1)$  blues. However,  $\textbf{by the end}$  of the  $r_1^{\text{th}}$  block, there is already  $(p-1)r_1 \geq (p-1)(p-a)a$  blues. 

By simple inequalities, we will derive that
\begin{align*} (p-1)(p-a)a &\geq (p-1)\left( \dfrac{p-a+1}{2} \right) \left( \dfrac{p+3}{2} \right)  &> (p-1) \left(\dfrac{p+1}{4}\right) (p-a+1) \end{align*}
utilizing  $a \geq \dfrac{p+3}{2}$  from the first Claim.

We are done.  $\blacksquare$   $\blacksquare$   $\blacksquare$  
--------

<details><summary>Very-unlikely-completion of Gaps.</summary>This is mostly motivated by Just Counting until some terms do not fit. 

Also, to simplify language I'm just going with  $\textit{large numbers}$  when talking about  $r_i$  ( $i$  large) instead of the more appropriate and deserving  $\textit{large averages}$  because in my workings,  $r_i$ 's size wasn't considered until much later; so I automatically identified those numbers as  $\textbf{bringing large quantities of reds}$  rather than  $\textit{larger in size or later in} \ 1 \ \textit{to} \ N$ .  $\color{green} \rule{25cm}{2pt}$   $\color{red} \text{Sec 1: Greedy and Near-Missing the Statement.}$  First I started with  $p = 5$ , where  $5$  blocks are available. This almost seemed plausible, until I was unable to create a  $1/5$  (the hints are given  $\textbf{\textit{this}}$  early, but it's very difficult to point out what's really wrong about completing  $4/5$  to  $1/5$ .) 

Since  $r(n)$  is written as  $a/p$  instead of  $\dfrac{a}{p}$ , so I adapted this as the notation  $\text{4 out of 5}$  seems more plausible than  $\dfrac{4}{5} \ \text{of all}$  --- since [list = disc] [*] the  $29$  numbers are nicely divided into  $1-5$ ,  $6-10$  and so on without any repercussions, as a  $\textit{point of completion}$  of  $a \in \{1,2,\ldots,p-1\}$  (which I called to be  $\textit{block-satisfiers}$  in my original Solution) can only occur nicely at the end of a block. This makes any other (artificial) grouping irrelevant, and [*] it seemed nice to say  $4/5$  in the first group to represent  $4$  red, without overly pushing away the prospect of considering  $5$  (total) -  $4$  (red) =  $1$  (the other color, blue). [/list]
Repeating the case with  $p = 7$ , I noted that completing the big  $\textit{block-satisfiers}$  prompted a size-issue with the smallest of block-satisfiers, as a  $6,4,2$  in the first three blocks completes  $r_6,r_5,r_4$ ; and also  $r_3$  after 4 blocks,  $r_2$  after 6 blocks, but we'd need an extra block to complete  $r_1$ . 

I repeated this not only for  $p = 11$ , until  $p$  not necessarily prime (all non-prime odds, and evens, too) and it seems that  $\dfrac{1}{4}n^2+O(n)$  blocks are theoretically needed to cancel the completion of  $r_i$ .  

For larger  $p$ , however, if  $\dfrac{p^2-1}{4}$ , I encountered some issues in handling the numbers from the  $\textit{small house}$  of  $r_1$  and beyond. For numbers as small as  $11$ , after filling out the greedily assigned 
\[ 10/11, 8/11, 6/11, 4/11, 2/11 \ \text{to complete} \ r_{10},r_9,\ldots,r_6 \]
I found out that  $r_5$  to  $r_1$  cannot be completed in  $30$  blocks; because if it can, then the total number of reds must be equal to  $30$  to warrant  $r_1$ 's completion, but  $r_4$  cannot be completed  $\textbf{without}$  adding at least  $2$  more reds after the fifth block. Then, I realized that the sum of  $10$  to  $2$  is what makes the deal, as the identity
\[ \dfrac{p^2-1}{4} = 2+4+6+\ldots+(p-1) \]
This invalidates any attempt to greedify the completion of the large numbers' house (or the small numbers too, for that matter, by the flipping argument) without assimilating it with some smaller numbers before some  $r_i$ ,  $i \geq 6$ .  $\color{green} \rule{25cm}{2pt}$   $\color{red} \text{Sec 2: Un-Greedying and Limited Options.}$  Regressing back a bit to the smaller case  $p = 7$  (in my experience, always good to revert for a harder case, as well) I tried to fulfill the large  $r_5$  and  $r_6$  by switching the order: what if  $r_5$  appears first? 

This turned out to be a very bad idea, since a  $5/7$  for  $r_5$  and  $7/7$  for  $r_6$ , this directly invalidates  $r_1$  due to there already being  $12$  reds in  $2$  blocks, while there must be  $r_1$  reds by the  $r_1^{\text{th}}$  block. 

A more enlightening consideration is for  $p = 11$ , where if  $r_{10}$  is as  $\textsf{big}$  as  $2$  (and spoiler alert:  $2$  is the second smallest natural number),  $r_1$  cannot appear in the first  $19$  blocks (while  $r_2, r_3,r_4$  definitely can).

So, there's almost no more slots for  $r_8$  (assuming  $r_9 = 1$ ) earlier than  $r_1$ , but there may be something later? What if there's some way for  $r_6$  and  $r_7$  to appear much later than  $r_1$ , but  $r_8$  somehow is unscathed? 

(Note: to comprehend this, I drew a picture of 3 rows of  $10$  brackets  $[11]$  to represent blocks of size  $11$ , but it was certainly daunting to have the best  $r_1$  possible cover two-thirds of the config --- in which room does the rest of the large numbers' house is? Since  $20$  reds are already booked, how far-off is adding another, say,  $4$  reds to complete  $r_6$ , or  $8$  reds, to complete  $r_7$ ?) 

I noted that the more I tried to artificially rearrange the extremes (i.e.  $r_{10},r_9,r_1$ ), the more questions I asked myself. This was amplified by considering divisibility problems; technically speaking, before  $r_1$ 's existence in the example above,  $20$  seems to be good for only its size; there's plenty more numbers (such as  $24$ , divisible by  $4,6,8$  which serves as a good standard for completing those averages.)  $\color{green} \rule{25cm}{2pt}$   $\color{red} \text{Sec 3: Both Houses Complete, and the Later House Prevails.}$  Still fixating on  $p = 11$ , I knew that  $r_{10}$  to  $r_6$  cannot wholly appear before  $r_1$ , but I didn't see what that can contribute for. The best I could come up was to consider when a house is fully complete (WLOG it's the big one), have  $r_1$  the extreme  $\textit{block-satisfier}$  in the middle, and try to complete the missing ones later. 

However, since there is a lack of clear distinction from the big house  $r_6$  to  $r_10$  and the small house  $r_5$  to  $r_1$ , I knew that  $\color{red} \clubsuit$   $\color{red} \boxed{\textbf{One Member from the Full-House Missing}}$   $\color{red} \clubsuit$  is what fundamentally separates the big and the small house; the scarcity of  $\dfrac{p^2-1}{4}-1$  blocks made it clear that the large house would have to be separated in some way. 

The more important question, (again) is  $\textbf{in what way}$ ? To answer that, I chose the most extreme way to proceed: what if I put  $r_{10}$ , then directly  $r_1$  after, before handling  $r_2$  and  $r_9$ ? 

This is by no way a free bound, since a 
\[ 1/11, 11/11, \ldots , 11/11 \ \text{with 9 full blocks of 11 blues} \]
is required even when  $r_{10} = 1$  (the smallest of naturals needs to be balanced by the tenth smallest.) At any rate, this isn't a surprising discovery, as we'd have a deficit of  $9$  blues in the first block to warrant a  $10/11$  blue average on the  $r_1^{\text{th}}$  block (note how size is getting started to be clearly considered here.) 

A clear observation after this is that  $r_2$  with  $9/11$  average on blue numbers can easily be achieved by adding a blue  $8/22$  after (for a  $108$  in 12 blocks), and similarly with  $r_3$  with a  $6/22$ , and so on. What's difficult is to obtain a natural  $r_9$  from an overflowing of  $100$  blues in the first  $10$  blocks; as it turns out, this is actually an impossible task.  $\color{green} \rule{25cm}{2pt}$   $\color{red} \text{Sec 3.1: Double Transition Equals Doom.}$  And that is only realized by noting that we need  $45 = \frac{90}{2}$  blocks to create a  $r_9$ . The size argument is then validated by the observation that  $\textbf{it takes time}$  to create a full  $r_{10}$  to  $r_a$ , and that time perpetuates a small number of total blues in a relatively large block --- and when this is carried over to  $r_1$  which requires a relatively large blue numbers, this quickly goes to ruins. 

As I'm guessing that it takes  $O(p)$  time (a.k.a. blocks) to go from  $1/p$  to  $p-1/p$ , I'd imagine it'll also take  $O(p) \cdot O(p)$  time to counteract the damage from the first  $O(p)$  blocks --- and this is surprisingly validated by the fact that  $a \geq \dfrac{p+3}{2}$  (a rephrase of not-full-house, as I mentioned in my Solution.)

<details><summary>Thoughts</summary>Suppose the contrary, since  $N$  is quite random for now, let's ignore its actual size, and make a few easy observations without it.

- If  $r(n)=\frac{a}{p}$ , then clearly  $n$  must be multiple of  $p$ . So it suffice to check  $r(ip)$  for all  $1\le i\le\lfloor \frac{N}{p}\rfloor=T$ . Note that  $T<\frac{p^2-1}{4}$ .

Let's consider the number of red points in the interval  $[ip+1, (i+1)p]$ , call it  $x_i$  for all  $1\le i \le T$ . My idea is that it will be easier for us not to look at red/blue points, and see it solely as a sequence problem. Note that we can reformulate the problem into the following:

''Let  $x_1, \cdots, x_T$  be integers between  $0$  to  $p$ , with  $T<\frac{p^2-1}{4}$ . Then define   $$ y_n=\frac{x_1+\cdots +x_n}{n} $$   We want to prove there is some integer  $1\le a\le p-1$  that doesn't appear in any of  $y_1, \cdots, y_T$ .''

The next idea is that  $y_n$  cannot change too drastically: If  $y_1=p-1$ , you clearly cannot expect  $y_2=1$ . This means there must be some bounds between  $y_i$  and  $y_j$ . Indeed, this hinges on the fact that  $0\le x_n\le p$ . 

Also, other non-integer  $y_n$  are kinda useless to what we intend to investigate about, so lets focus only on those that are integers. So suppose for the sake of a contradiction, that there are indices  $1\le t_1, \cdots t_{p-1} \le T$  with  $y_{t_i}=i$  for all  $1\le i\le p-1$ .

- Using  $0\le x_n\le p$ , I could deduce two pairs of interesting inequalities relating  $t_i$  and  $t_j$  for all  $i, j$ , One pair is obvious using  $x_n\ge 0$ ;   $$ t_i<t_j \Rightarrow it_i\le jt_j \hspace{3mm} \text{and} \hspace{3mm} t_i>t_j \Rightarrow it_i\ge jt_j $$   
The other involves a nice algebraic trick using  $p-x_n$ , and we get a symmetrical result that   $$ t_i<t_j \Rightarrow (p-i)t_i\le (p-j)t_j \hspace{3mm} \text{and} \hspace{3mm} t_i>t_j \Rightarrow (p-i)t_i\ge (p-j)t_j $$   This also corresponds to swapping the colors in the original setting!

With these, our claim is that we can't fit in  $t_1, \cdots, t_{p-1}$  within  $[1, \frac{p^2-1}{4}-1]$ . Now for the visualization - place everything on a number line. 

The picture is that whenever we have two  $t_i<t_j$ , then this ordering is getting pushed even further by the two inequalities above. Obviously, this ''pushing'' effect is most obvious with  $1$  and  $p-1$ : Either  $t_1<t_{p-1}\Rightarrow (p-1)t_1<t_{p-1}$  or  $t_1>t_{p-1}\Rightarrow t_1>(p-1)t_{p-1}$ . So perhaps we should focus on one of these two.

Unfortunately, in both cases, the pushing effect only gave us a range of order  $p$  only. We need more than that. Let's be more consistent with the direction of the pushing: With the  $p-x_n$  symmetry, we can assume  $t_1<t_{p-1}$ . Then, intuitively, we want to push  $t_{p-1}$  to the right, and if there are more things on the left of  $t_{p-1}$ , we hope to push  $t_{p-1}$  even further. But how?

The idea is we ''scan'' again! (Notice how simple yet versatile ideas can really help a lot, compared to some obscure but rare ones!) Consider  $t_1<t_{p-1}, t_2<t_{p-1}, \cdots, t_k<t_{p-1}$  up to some  $k$ . I claim that this pushes  $t_{p-1}$  roughly to order  $k(p-k)$  now, which is optimal when  $k=\frac{p-1}{2}$ .

- Turns out if  $t_{p-1}>t_i$  for all  $1\le i\le \frac{p-1}{2}$ , then we get a contradiction by considering the rightmost of  $t_1, \cdots, t_{\frac{p-1}{2}}$ , This is because this rightmost term turns out to be the one that actually pushes  $t_{p-1}$  the most!

- If we stop at some  $k< \frac{p-1}{2}$ , that's okay, because  $t_{p-1}$  will then push  $t_{k+1}$  very far away to the right, again by considering the rightmost of  $t_1, \cdots, t_k$  to push  $t_{p-1}$  to the right first.

\[B_{i+1}\ge (b_{i+1}) \left\lceil \frac{B_i}{b_{i+1}}\right\rceil\]
so  $A_{i+1}\ge (a_{i+1}) \left\lceil \tfrac{B_i}{b_{i+1}}\right\rceil$ . It is similar when  $b_{i+1}>b_i$ .  $~$ Given fixed sequences  $a$  and  $b$ , choosing greedily always proves to be optimal. Inductively, this is simple. If  $A_{i}$  and  $B_{i}$  are greater than the value obtain greedily, then  $B_{i+1}$  necessarily will be, and by proportionality so will  $A_{i+1}$ . In particular, the local proportionality of  $A$  and  $B$  ensures that our argument works regardless of whether  $b_{i+1}>b_i$  or  $a_{i+1}>a_i$ . $~$ Thus, we can assume that the following algorithm is used to optimally construct  $A$  and  $B$  using a given  $a$  and  $b$ :  $A_1=a_1$  and  $B_1=b_1$ . If  $k \geq \frac{p-1}{2}$ , then among  $p-1,\ldots,\frac{p+1}{2}$  at least one has index  $\geq \frac{p-1}{2}$ , because  $b_i \geq i$ ,  $m \geq \frac{p-1}{2} \frac{p+1}{2}=\frac{p^2-1}{4}>\frac{p^2-5}{4}$  - contradiction. So  $k \leq \frac{p-3}{2}$ . If  $p=3$ ,  $1 \leq k \leq 0$  - contradiction, so  $p \geq 5$ . Now also do the same argument with  $p-1,\ldots,p-k$ , so  $m \geq k(p-k)$ Now consider the second chain of inequalities. We know that  $p-k-1=c_r$ , where  $r>a$ , so  $p-c_r=k+1$ . Then  $(p-1)m \leq (k+1)b_r$ , so  $\frac{p^2-1}{4} > b_r \geq \frac{(p-1)m}{k+1} \geq \frac{(p-1)k(p-k)}{k+1}$ , so  $(p+1)(k+1) > 4k(p-k)$ , so  $$ 4k^2-(3p-1)k+(p+1)>0 $$  This function of  $k$  is convex, so it's maximum on the segment  $[1,\frac{p-3}{2}]$  must be in one of it's endpoints.  $k=1$ : $4-(3p-1)+(p+1)>0$ , which rewrites as  $p<3$  - false.  $k=\frac{p-3}{2}$ : $2(p-3)^2-(3p-1)(p-3)+2(p+1)>0$  $2p^2-12p+18-3p^2+10p-3+2p+2>0$ , which rewrites as  $p^2<17$  - false

Prove that the elements of  $\mathcal{S}$  may be ordered as  $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$  so that  $a_i$  does not divide  $a_{i - 1} + a_{i + 1}$  for all  $i = 2, 3, \dots, n - 1$ .
solution_md:
We'll prove the following statement by proceeding induction on  $n$ :

Let  $S$  be a set consisting of  $n \ge 3$  positive integers, none of which is a sum of two other distinct elements of  $S$ . Then, we can order the elements of  $S$  as  $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$  so that  $a_i \nmid a_{i-1} + a_{i+1}$  and  $a_i \nmid a_{i-1} - a_{i+1}$  for all  $2 \le i \le n-1$ . 

Base case   $n = 3$  is clear. Now assume it's true on  $n-1$  and lets prove on  $n$ . Let  $a = \max(S)$ . By induction hypothesis, we may assume that the elements of  $S\backslash \{a\}$  can be ordered as  $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_{n-1}$  so that  $a_i \nmid a_{i-1} + a_{i+1}$  and  $a_i \nmid a_{i-1} - a_{i+1}$  for all  $2 \le i \le n-2$ . Our goal is to find an integer  $i$  such that the sequence  $(a_1, a_2, \dots, a_{i}, a, a_{i+1}, \dots, a_n)$  satisfies the condition.

Note that for any  $\varepsilon_1, \varepsilon_2 \in \{-1, 1\}, a_k \mid a + \varepsilon_1a_{k-1}$  and  $a_k \mid a + \varepsilon_2a_{k+1}$  cannot simultaneously hold, otherwise we get  $a_k \mid a_{k-1} + \varepsilon a_{k+1}$  for some  $\varepsilon \in \{-1, 1\}$ , a contradiction.

Call an integer  $k$  is left if  $a_k \mid a + \varepsilon a_{k-1}$  for some  $\varepsilon \in \{-1, 1\}$  and call it right if  $a_k \mid a + \varepsilon a_{k-1}$  and call it good otherwise. Then, note that  $1$  has to be left and  $n-1$  has to be right, otherwise, we may insert  $a$  into beginning or ending of the sequence  $(a_1, a_2, \dots, a_{n-1})$ . If there is an integer  $k$  such that  $k$  is not right and  $k+1$  is not left, then we may insert  $a$  into  $(a_k, a_{k+1})$ . Exclude all good indices as they are irrelevant. Then, since  $1$  is left and  $n-1$  is right, at some point, there is an integer  $k$  such that  $k$  is left and  $k+1$  is right. Thus, we can insert  $a$  into  $(a_k, a_{k+1})$  and  add good numbers we erased, we get our desired permutation. Hence, our induction step is completed, so we're done.  $\blacksquare$ **Remark:** All motivation came from checking little cases as  $n = 3,4,5$ . While checking  $n=4,5$ , it motivates a deeper focus on size arguments, which led me to generalize the problem statement. Also, after reading the problem, induction instantly came into my head and the generalized problem wasn't so hard to prove.  :D

SolutionLet the elements of $\mathcal{S}$ be $x_1 < x_2 < \cdots < x_n$ . **Claim:** $x_n$ can never divide the sum of its neighbors. *Proof*. Assume for contradiction that $x_n \mid x_i + x_j$ (with $i < j < n$ ). Then $x_i + x_j \neq x_n$ , so we must have $x_i + x_j \geq 2x_n$ , but this is a size contradiction, as $x_i$ and $x_j$ are strictly smaller than $x_n$ . $\blacksquare$ **Claim:** For any $k < \ell$ , there is at most one $i < k$ for which $x_k \mid x_i + x_\ell$ . *Proof*. Assume that $x_k$ divides both $x_i + x_\ell$ and $x_j + x_\ell$ , wth $i < j < k$ . Then $x_k$ must divide $x_j - x_i$ . But this is strictly less than $x_k$ , contradiction. $\blacksquare$ Now first write down $x_n$ . We're going to take $x_{n - 1}$ , $x_{n - 2}$ , $\ldots$ in that order, and add them to either the left end or the right end of the sequence -- this creates a sequence that is increasing up to $x_n$ , and then decreasing. It suffices to do this so that we never have $x_j \mid x_i + x_k$ , where $x_i < x_j < x_k$ are the three most recent numbers we placed on a side. To add the numbers, use the following process: first keep adding numbers to the left until stuck (meaning that $x_j \mid x_i + x_k$ , so we can't add $x_i$ ). Then keep adding numbers to the right until stuck (we can add at least one number here, because the first number added on either side has no condition to check). Then keep adding numbers to the left until stuck (we can add at least one because $x_j \mid x_i + x_k$ , so $x_j$ doesn't divide $x_\ell + x_k$ for the current $\ell < i$ that we're on). Then keep adding numbers to the right until stuck (we can add at least one for the same reason). Keep doing this until we've placed all the numbers -- the second claim means that we can place at least one number every time we switch, and that after that the side we left becomes safe again. So eventually we can place everything. **Remark:** The main idea is that we can get the second claim for triples $x_k \mid x_i + x_\ell$ where $i < k < \ell$ (this was motivated by thinking about the $n = 4$ case, where we want to place $x_3$ and $x_4$ in the middle, and we win as long as $x_3$ doesn't divide both $x_4 + x_1$ and $x_4 + x_2$ ), but it's a lot harder to say anything about $x_k \mid x_i + x_\ell$ where $k < i, \ell$ . So we'd like to find a sequence that avoids this entirely, which means it must go up and then down.

Let $\mathcal{S}$ be a set consisting of $n \ge 3$ positive integers, none of which is a sum of two other distinct members of $\mathcal{S}$ . Prove that the elements of $\mathcal{S}$ may be ordered as $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ so that $a_i$ does not divide $a_{i - 1} + a_{i + 1}$ for all $i = 2, 3, \dots, n - 1$ .
We inductively prove this statement, with the base case clear. Assume that there is such an ordering for \(\mathcal{S}\) with cardinality \(n\), and let the ordering be \[\{a_1,a_2,\hdots,a_n\}\] Now we need to show that we can place \(a_{n+1}>\max\{a_1,a_2,\hdots,a_n\}\) in such a way that the condition of the statement holds true with one of the elements being \(a_{n+1}\). Firstly, we cannot have \(a_{n+1}\mid a_i+a_j\) for any \(i,j\) (need not be consecutive), because \(a_i+a_j<2a_{n+1}\) and \(a_i+a_j\) cannot be equal to \(a_{n+1}\), since \(\mathcal{S}\) is sum-free. Now, assume for the sake of contradiction that we cannot place \(a_{n+1}\) between any two consecutive terms \(a_i\) and \(a_{i+1}\), i.e. \(a_i\mid a_{n+1}+a_{i+1}\) or \(a_{i+1}\mid a_{n+1}+a_{i+2}\) (the case \(a_{n+1}\mid a_i+a_{i+1}\) being excluded due to what we proved above). I emphasize on **or** because both the statements cannot be true at once: If they were both true then we get \(a_i\mid a_{i-1}+a_{i+1}\) contradicting our inductive assumption. Therefore, one of them is true and the other is false. Therefore, we must have that \(a_i\mid a_{i+1}+a_{n+1} \) for all \(2\leq i\leq n-1\) and \(a_i\nmid a_{i-1}+a_{n+1}\) for all \(2\leq i\leq n\) (\(a_2\mid a_3+a_{n+1}\) implies that \(a_3\mid a_4+a_{n+1}\) because \(a_{2}\nmid a_1+a_{n+1}\) and so on). But that means that \(a_{n-1}\nmid a_{n-2}+a_{n+1}\) and so if we place \(a_{n+1}\) in the middle of \(a_{n-1}\) and \(a_n\), we get that that particular ordering indeed satisfies the statement of the problem, contradicting the assumption that no matter where you place \(a_{n+1}\) the statement fails. This completes the proof of the problem.
Motivational CommentsThe divisibility relation should immediately trigger induction, because the statement of the problem could be "burned" into a divisibility problem where you have one term fixed in all the divisibilities. Once you have achieved this idea, the rest all is some elegant casework (unlike many problems which are so bashy and annoying). We basically get three cases to handle, \(a\mid b+c\), \(b\mid c+a\) or \(c\mid a+b\). We rule out one of the divisibility conditions by assuming that \(a_{n+1}\) is the largest among them all, so we have two cases to handle and it isn't that hard to show that one of them work. Also, since we must have \(a_1\mid a_2+a_{n+1}\), the other divisibilities follow chainly, like how dominoes roll over as soon as you just push one of them. In the end I got to some divisibility conditions and found that they alone wouldnt help (like tried ineqs, substituting,... but all of them were so disgusting expressions). Then when I thought of the relations I neglected, I see that the chain works there too, so in the end what actually mattered was the relations that I negated which led me to the final non-divisibility relation solving the problem!
RemarksThis is kind of easy for a N7, but indeed it is a very tricky problem where the relations most people neglect is the most crucial step for the conclusion of the problem.

First, order the elements of  $S$  in decreasing order  $a_1>a_2>a_3> \dots > a_n.$  We then make two crucial observations: ***Lemma 1: Let  $2 \le i,j \le n$  be two distinct indexes, then  $a_1 \nmid a_i+ a_j.$***
*<u>Proof</u>:*
Since  $a_1$  is maximal, we must have  $a_1 > {a_i}{/2} + {a_j}{/2};$  and by problems condition  $a_1 \ne a_i + a_j$  so the result follows.

***Lemma 2: Let  $i$  and  $j$  be any distinct indexes; then the number of indexes  $i<k\le n$  such that  $a_i \mid a_k+ a_j$  is at most 1***
<u>*Proof:*</u>
Suppose otherwise that,  $a_i \mid a_k+ a_j$  and  $a_i \mid a_l+ a_j$  for distinct indexes  $i <k,l\le n.$  Then,  $a_i \mid |a_k - a_l|;$  hence, since  $a_k \ne a_l,$  we must have  $a_i \le |a_k - a_l|,$  which is absurd since  $a_i >a_k,a_l.$ Now we will order the sequence such that it satisfies problems condition. Start with the sequence  $a_1;$  we will say that a sequence is *valid*if it satisties problems condition. We will add the numbers  $a_2,a_3,\dots, a_n,$  "one by one" such that the sequence continues valid. We perform the following algorithm: $\bullet$  At first, let  $i_1$  be the maximal such that the sequence  $a_1,\dots , a_{i_1}$ is *valid;* if  $i_1 = n$  we finish the algorithm. $\bullet$  For  $j \ge 2,$  at the  $j^{th}$  step of the algorithm (if it has not finished yet), if  $j$  is even(respectively odd) we add the numbers  $a_{i_{j-1} +1},\dots , a_{i_j}$  to the left (respectively right) of the sequence; if  $i_j = n,$  we stop the algorithm.

For showing the algorithm works until we reach  $n,$  we only need to show  $i_j \ge i_{j-1} + 1$  for all  $j.$  Indeed, we have that  $i_2 \ge i_1$  since if  $i_1 \ne n,$  we can add the number  $a_{i_1+1}$  to the left of the sequence keeping it *valid* unless  $a_1 \mid a_{2} + a_{i_1+1},$  which cannot happen by *Lemma 1,*. Now, we proceed by induction, assume we have contructed the sequence up to the  $j^{th}$  step without finish or get stucked; then we must have by construction  $$  a_{i_{j-1}} \mid a_{i_{j-1}-1} + a_{i_{j-1}+1} $$  Hence, by *Lemma 2,* we have   $$ a_{i_{j-1}} \nmid a_{i_{j-1}-1} + a_{ i_j+1} $$  since by induction hiphothesis  $i_j + 1 > i_{j-1} +1;$  so we can add  $a_{ i_j+1}$  to the sequence thus  $i_{j+1} \ge i_j +1.$  So the algorithm works.

Call such an order a *cute* order. If  $n = 3$ , it is possible as, if the numbers are  $a < b < c$ , then  $c \nmid a+b$  as  $c \neq a+b$  and  $2c > a+b$ .

Suppose its true until  $n$ , I'll show it for  $n+1$ , let  $M$  be the maximum of the numbers, and by induction let the remaining numbers be ordered  $a_1, a_2, \cdots, a_n$ . I claim there exists a way to add  $M$  while still keeping the ordering cute.

First, note that  $M$  cannot divide the sum of any two other elements as the set is sum free and  $M$  is the maximum. Try to place  $M$  in between  $a_1$  and  $a_2$ , if this makes the ordering not cute, then it must be that  $a_2 | M + a_3$ . By induction I claim that  $a_i | M + a_{i+1}$  for all  $2 \leqslant i \leqslant n-1$ . The base case is done so for the inductive step suppose its true for  $i = 2,3,\cdots,k-1$  and we need it for  $k$ . Note that if placing  $M$  between  $a_{k-1}$  and  $a_k$  causes a problem, then either  $a_{k-1} | M + a_{k-2}$  or  $a_k | M + a_{k+1}$ . But since  $a_{k-1} | M+a_k$  by induction, it follows that  $a_{k-1} | a_{k} - a_{k-2}$ . It would be nice if this led to a contradiction but it unfortunately does not. But not all is lost. 

To remedy this, we will actually induct on the stronger hypothesis that you can order the elements such that each element divides neither the sum *nor the difference* of its neighbors. Now, similar to the above paragraph, but to simplify things, call a pair  $(i,i+1)$  or  $(i,i-1)$  *annoying* if  $a_i | a_{i \pm 1} \pm M$  and  $2 \leqslant i \leqslant n-1$ . Note that we cannot have  $a_i | a_{i-1} \pm M$  *and*  $a_i | a_{i+1} \pm M$ , as if both have the same sign, then  $a_i | a_{i+1} - a_{i-1}$ , impossible by induction, and if both have opposite signs, then  $a_i | a_{i-1} + a_{i+1}$ , again impossible by induction.

Consider inserting  $M$  in any of  $n-1$  places - after  $a_1$  or after  $a_2$  until after  $a_{n-1}$ . An annoying pair can be seen to eliminate exactly one such position. But since for a fixed  $i$ , it can be annoying with at most one of its neighbours by the above paragraph, it follows that there are at most  $n-2$  annoying pairs, and since there are  $n-1$  positions, it follows that there exists a position where  $a_n$  can be inserted, completing the induction.  $\blacksquare$

Note that for two elements  $a,b$ , if  $a>b$  then  $a,b,c$  and  $c,b,a$  can be problematic for at most one element  $c<b$ , and if  $a<b$  then  $a,b,c$  and  $c,b,a$  can be problematic for  $0$  elements  $c<b$  because that would require  $b=a+c$ . Thus, we may start with the largest element, put the second largest element on one side of it and keep adding elements to that side (going in decreasing order always) until we get an element for which we cannot. Now, we are guaranteed to be able to put it on the other side, and the for the side which we could not put it all smaller elements can go there so we just keep adding elements to the other side until we cannot, then switch back to the original side and add elements until we cannot,  and so forth. This process is then guaranteed to end and work.

We induct on $n \ge 3$ . **Base case:** Set $n=3$ . Then, let $S=\{a, b, c\}$ , where $a**Inductive step:** Let $S=\{a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n\}$ , where $a_i$ is a strictly increasing sequence. stem_md:
In a dance party initially there are  $20$  girls and  $22$  boys in the pool and infinitely many more girls and boys waiting outside. In each round, a participant is picked uniformly at random; if a girl is picked, then she invites a boy from the pool to dance and then both of them elave the party after the dance; while if a boy is picked, then he invites a girl and a boy from the waiting line and dance together. The three of them all stay after the dance. The party is over when there are only (two) boys left in the pool.

(a) What is the probability that the party never ends?

(b) Now the organizer of this party decides to reverse the rule, namely that if a girl is picked, then she invites a boy and a girl from the waiting line to dance and the three stay after the dance; while if a boy is picked, he invites a girl from the pool to dance and both leave after the dance. Still the party is over when there are only (two) boys left in the pool. What is the expected number of rounds until the party ends?
solution_md:
<details><summary>answer to a)</summary>$\frac{20}{21}$</details>
<details><summary>Solution to a)</summary>This problem is similar to 2020 Alibaba C02. The invariant there is  $b$ , and the invariant here is  $\#(boys)-\#(girls)$ .

We can treat this process as a walk on a line. I start at  $x=20$ . Every minute, I either move left or right. If I move left (i.e. a girl and boy leaves), then a girl is chosen, with probability  $\frac{x}{2x+2}=\frac 12 \frac{x}{x+1}$ . It moves right with probability  $\frac 12 \frac{x+2}{x+1}$ We can use telescoping to see the probability of a walk with  $s$  steps that makes it end up  $d$  steps to the right is simply  $$ 2^{-s} \cdot \frac{x+d+1}{x+1} $$  (note if I drop the  $2^{-s}$ , a LR and RL cancels themselves)

Let  $f_d(t)$  be the number of walks from  $(0,0)$  to  $(t-d,t)$  staying entirely below (or on) the line  $y=x+d$ . We are trying to find  $1-\frac{1}{21} 2^{-19}\sum\limits_{t\ge 19} f_{19}(t) 4^{-t}$ I claim  $2^d \sum\limits_{t\ge d} f_d(t) 4^{-t}=2$ By the definition of Catalan numbers,  $f_0(t)=f_1(t)=C_t$ We can use casework to determine $C_t=\sum\limits_{i=0}^{k-2} f_i(t-1)+f_k(t)$  by noticing this is equivalent to going from  $(-d,0)$  to  $(t-d,t)$  and I can't go to  $(a,1)$  for any  $a<0$ .

Now we induct on  $d$ . The base case,  $d=1$  is clear by the Catalan generating function  $\sum\limits_{n\ge 1} C_nx^n=-1+\frac{1-\sqrt{1-4x}}{2x}|_{x=\frac 14}=1$ Inductive step:   $$ 2^k\sum\limits_{t\ge k} f_k(t)4^{-t} = 2^k \sum\limits_{t\ge k} (C_t-\sum\limits_{i=0}^{k-2} f_i(t-1))4^{-t} = 2^k(\sum_{t\ge k} C_t4^{-t} - \sum\limits_{i=0}^{k-2} \sum_{t\ge k} f_i(t-1)4^{-t}) $$    $$ \sum_{t\ge k} f_i(t-1)4^{-t}=\sum\limits_{t>i} f_i(t-1)4^{-t} - \sum_{t=i+1}^{k-1} f_i(t-1)4^{-t} $$    $$ \sum\limits_{t>i} f_i(t-1)4^{-t}=\frac 14\sum\limits_{t\ge i} f_i(t)4^{-t} = 2^{-i-1} $$   by inductive hypothesis.

Therefore,  $2^k(\sum_{t\ge k} C_t4^{-t} - \sum\limits_{i=0}^{k-2} \sum_{t\ge k} f_i(t-1)4^{-t})=2+2^k(\sum_{t=1}^{k-1} (c_t-\sum_{i=0}^{t-1} f_i(t-1))4^{-t})=2$ Note  $(c_t-\sum_{i=0}^{t-1} f_i(t-1))=0$  by caseworking on the smallest  $x$  such that  $(x,1)$  is reached.

Now, back to the original problem. Note  $f_{19}(t)$  is the number of paths from  $(0,0)$  to  $(t-19,t+1)$  where I touch the line  $y=x+20$  only at the last step. Note the probability that I touch the line  $y=x+20$  (i.e. the process stops) after  $t$  steps is  $f_{19}(t) 2^{-(t-19+t+1)}$ , so we get  $1-\frac{1}{21} 2^{18}\sum\limits_{t\ge 19} f_{19}(t) 4^{-t}=\frac{20}{21}$</details>

stem_md:
Consider a computer network consisting of servers and bi-directional communication channels among them. Unfortunately, not all channels operate. Each direction of each channel fails with probability  $p$  and operates otherwise. (All of these stochastic events are mutually independent, and  $0 \le p \le 1$ .) There is a root serve, denoted by  $r$ . We call the network *operational*, if all serves can reach  $r$  using only operating channels. Note that we do not require  $r$  to be able to reach any servers. 

Show that the probability of the network to be operational does not depend on the choice of  $r$ . (In other words, for any two distinct root servers  $r_1$  and  $r_2$ , the operational probability is the same.)
solution_md:
<details><summary>Solution</summary>**Lemma.** Let  $G$  be an undirected graph. The number of DAGs obtained by orienting each edge such that all vertices can go to root  $r_1$  is equal to the number of DAGs obtained by orienting each edge such all vertices can go to root  $r_2$  using directed edges.

Proof: We construct a bijection between the two types of DAGs to show the number of DAGs such that all vertices can go to root  $r_1$  is at most those that can go to root  $r_2$ .

Fix a DAG rooted at  $r_1$ , call  $G$ . Let  $X$  be the set of vertices in some path from  $r_2$  to  $r_1$ , and let  $Y$  be the other vertices. Note that  $G[X]$  is a graph with a unique source  $r_2$  and sink  $r_1$ , and there are no edges from  $X$  to  $Y$ . We flip all edges of  $G[X]$ . This produces a DAG rooted at  $r_2$  because all the other edges aren't affected, so they can go to a vertex whose edges may have been flipped, and go to  $r_2$ , which is doable because this vertex is originally on the path from  $r_1$  to  $r_2$ . If I do an analogous procedure on the changed graph, I get my original graph. **Now, back to the main problem.** I claim this problem is still true if the probability  $u\rightarrow v$  works is equal to the probability  $v\rightarrow u$  works. Let  $G$  be the counterexample with minimal vertices, and among them, the one with minimal edges.

First of all, if I'm given that  $u\rightarrow v, v\rightarrow u$  are both turned off, I'm working with a smaller graph, so this statement is true.

Secondly, if there is a cycle  $v_1\rightarrow v_2\rightarrow \cdots \rightarrow v_n\rightarrow v_1$ , then if I merge all those vertices into one, and also merge the probabilities (for example, if  $v_1q$  has a chance  $p_1$  of failing,  $v_2q$  has a chance  $p_2$  of failing, and all other vertices aren't adjacent to vertex  $q$ , then this new edge has  $p_1p_2$  chance of failing in either direction)

(We can use the Principle of Inclusion-Exclusion on those two cases, and find out any combination of the two gives a smaller counterexample. Therefore, we don't need to worry about those cases at all)

The only other possibility is considering the DAGs where for each edge, exactly one of  $u\rightarrow v, v\rightarrow u$  works. The probability that exactly one of  $u\rightarrow v, v\rightarrow u$  works is  $\prod\limits_{u,v \text{edge}} 2(1-p_{uv})p_{uv}$ , which doesn't depend on the vertex itself. Therefore, we multiply by the number of DAGs going to that vertex to get the probability for each vertex. By the lemma in the beginning, we are done.</details>

Given positive integers  $k \ge 2$  and  $m$  sufficiently large. Let  $\mathcal{F}_m$  be the infinite family of all the (not necessarily square) binary matrices which contain exactly  $m$  1's. Denote by  $f(m)$  the maximum integer  $L$  such that for every matrix  $A \in \mathcal{F}_m$ , there always exists a binary matrix  $B$  of the same dimension such that (1)  $B$  has at least  $L$  1-entries; (2) every entry of  $B$  is less or equal to the corresponding entry of  $A$ ; (3)  $B$  does not contain any  $k \times k$  all-1 submatrix. Show the equality
\[\lim_{m \to \infty} \frac{\ln f(m)}{\ln m}=\frac{k}{k+1}.\]
solution_md:
Saw this post by accident. Nice problem! Sorry for posting Chinese, but I dont have time for translation. This is the answer I wrote during the contest. Maybe with few typos.
Restate the original problem in graph-theoretic language: Let $f(m)$ be the largest integer $L$ , such that for any bipartite graph with exactly $m$ edges, there exists a subgraph with $L$ edges that does not contain a complete bipartite graph $K_{k, k}$ as a subgraph. First, I will prove that $\lim \frac{\ln f(m)}{\ln m} \geqslant \frac{k}{k+1}$ . Consider the maximum number of $K_{k, k}$ subgraphs in a bipartite graph with $m$ edges. For each subgraph isomorphic to $K_{k, k}$ , we can choose a perfect matching of size $k$ , which forms a $k$ -element subset of the original $m$ edges. Obviously, different $K_{k, k}$ subgraphs (as subgraphs) cannot select the same matching, so the number of subgraphs isomorphic to $K_{k, k}$ is at most $\binom{m}{k} < m^k$ . Let $p = \frac{m^{-\frac{1}{k+1}}}{2}$ . Let $G = \left(V_1, V_2\right)$ be an arbitrary bipartite graph with exactly $m$ edges. For each edge of $G$ , independently choose whether it belongs to set $S$ with probability $p$ . Then, $\mathbb{E}(|S|) = p m = \frac{m^{\frac{k}{k+1}}}{2}$ , and the edges of $S$ will determine a subgraph of $G$ . I calculate the expected number of $K_{k, k}$ subgraphs contained in this subgraph. For each $K_{k, k}$ contained in $G$ , it is included in $S$ with probability $p^{k^2}$ . The number of such subgraphs does not exceed $m^k$ , so by the additivity of expectation, the expected number of $K_{k, k}$ subgraphs in $S$ does not exceed $p^{k^2} m^k = \frac{m^{\frac{k}{k+1}}}{2^{k^2}}$ . By Markov's inequality, the probability that $S$ contains more than $\frac{2 m^{\frac{k}{k+1}}}{2^{k^2}}$ $K_{k, k}$ subgraphs is at most $\frac{1}{2}$ . Next, consider the distribution of the number of edges in $S$ (i.e., $|S|$ ). By the Central Limit Theorem, with high probability, it falls within $\mathbb{E}(S) \pm O(\sqrt{m p})$ (specifically, when $m$ is large enough, the probability that $S$ belongs to $[\mathbb{E}(S) - \sqrt{m p}, \mathbb{E}(S) + \sqrt{m p}]$ is greater than $\frac{1}{2}$ ). Therefore, there is a choice of $S$ that simultaneously satisfies: $|S| \geqslant \mathbb{E}(S) - \sqrt{m p}$ and the number of $K_{k, k}$ subgraphs in $S$ does not exceed $\frac{2 m^{\frac{k}{k+1}}}{2^{k^2}}$ . For each such subgraph, remove one edge from $S$ to obtain a set denoted by $S'$ . Then $S'$ contains no subgraph isomorphic to $K_{k, k}$ . Furthermore, \[ |S'| \geqslant \mathbb{E}(S) - \sqrt{m p} - \frac{2 m^{\frac{k}{k+1}}}{2^{k^2}} = \frac{m^{\frac{k}{k+1}}}{2} - \sqrt{m p} - \frac{2 m^{\frac{k}{k+1}}}{2^{k^2}} = O\left(m^{\frac{k}{k+1}}\right) \] Therefore, $\lim \frac{\ln f(m)}{\ln m} \geqslant \frac{k}{k+1}$ . Now, I will prove $\lim \frac{\ln f(m)}{\ln m} \leqslant \frac{k}{k+1}$ . Note that the condition "exactly $m$ edges" can be changed to "at least $m$ edges" in this case. Removing edges will not increase the maximum integer $L$ . Consider the complete bipartite graph $G$ with left and right vertex sets of sizes $V_1 = \left\lceil m^{\frac{k}{k+1}} \right\rceil$ and $V_2 = \left\lceil m^{\frac{1}{k+1}} \right\rceil$ . Let $H$ be a subgraph of $G$ that does not contain $K_{k, k}$ . Let $X \subseteq V_1$ be the set of vertices in $V_1$ with at least $k$ neighbors in $H$ . For each $x \in X$ , choose a $k$ -element subset $Y_x \subseteq V_2$ from its neighbors. Since $H$ does not contain $K_{k, k}$ , each $k$ -element subset of $V_2$ can appear at most $k-1$ times. Therefore, $|X| \leqslant (k-1) \binom{|V_2|}{k} < (k-1)\left(m^{\frac{1}{k+1}} + 1\right)^k$ . The number of neighbors of each vertex in $V_1 \backslash X$ does not exceed $k-1$ . Thus: \[ |E(H)| < (k-1)\left(m^{\frac{1}{k+1}} + 1\right)^k + (k-1)|V_1| < \operatorname{poly}(k) \cdot m^{\frac{k}{k+1}} \] Therefore, $\lim \frac{\ln f(m)}{\ln m} \leqslant \frac{k}{k+1}$ .

Consider a bipartite graph with exactly \(m\) edges and look at the maximum possible number of subgraphs isomorphic to \(K_{k,k}\).  For each such subgraph, one can pick out a perfect matching of size \(k\) (that is, a \(k\)-element subset of the original \(m\) edges).  Clearly, two distinct copies of \(K_{k,k}\) cannot share exactly the *same* \(k\)-element matching, so the total number of \(K_{k,k}\)-subgraphs is at most \(\binom{m}{k}\).

Next, let \(G = (V_1, V_2)\) be a bipartite graph with exactly \(m\) edges, and let
\[
p \;=\; \text{[some function of  $m$ ]}.
\]  
Independently include each edge of \(G\) in a random subset \(S\) with probability \(p\).  Then the expected size of \(S\) is \(\mathbb{E}[|S|] = pm.\)  One can check (by standard counting) that the expected number of copies of \(K_{k,k}\) inside the subgraph induced by \(S\) is at most
\(\binom{m}{k}\,p^{\,k^2}.\)  
By Markov’s inequality, the probability that \(S\) contains *more* than 
\(2\,\binom{m}{k}\,p^{\,k^2}\) copies of \(K_{k,k}\) is at most \(1/2\).

We also look at the distribution of \(|S|\).  By a central limit theorem (or Chernoff bound) argument, \(|S|\) is highly likely to lie in the interval 
\[
\bigl(pm - O\bigl(\sqrt{mp}\bigr),\; pm + O\bigl(\sqrt{mp}\bigr)\bigr).
\]  
Concretely, for sufficiently large \(m\), the probability that 
\(\,|S| \ge pm - \sqrt{mp}\) 
exceeds \(1/2\).  Therefore, there is a particular way of choosing the edges in \(S\) so that 
\[
|S| \;\ge\; pm - \sqrt{mp}
\quad\text{and}\quad
\text{(\# of  $K_{k,k}$  subgraphs in  $S$ )} \;\le\; 2\,\binom{m}{k}\,p^{\,k^2}.
\]
From such an \(S\), we can (if necessary) remove edges one by one (and collect them into a new set \(S'\)) to eliminate these unwanted \(K_{k,k}\).  A rough estimate shows
\[
|S'|
\;\ge\;
\bigl(pm - \sqrt{mp}\bigr)\;-\;\bigl[\text{at most }k\cdot 2\,\binom{m}{k}\,p^{\,k^2}\bigr],
\]
and by choosing \(p\) appropriately in terms of \(m\), one can make this large enough to yield
\[
\liminf_{m \to \infty}\,\frac{\ln f(m)}{n\,m} \;\ge\; \frac{k}{k+1}.
\]

For the opposite direction, consider a bipartite graph *not* containing \(K_{k,k}\).  Take the left and right vertex sets to have sizes \(\lfloor m^{\frac{k+1}{k}}\rfloor\) each, forming a complete bipartite graph on those two sets.  Let \(X \subseteq V_1\) be the set of vertices in the left part that have degree at least \(k\).  From each vertex \(x \in X\), pick some \(k\)-element subset of its neighbors in \(V_2.\)  Because the overall graph does not contain \(K_{k,k}\), each vertex in \(V_2\) can appear in at most \((k-1)\) of these chosen subsets.  Hence the size of \(X\) is at most \(\binom{|V_2|}{k}\), which is in turn bounded by something like 
\((k-1)\bigl(m^{\tfrac{k+1}{k}} + 1\bigr)^{k}.\)  
Meanwhile, every vertex in \(V_1\setminus X\) has degree at most \(k-1\).  
Putting this together shows that the total number of edges in such a graph is
\[
E(H)
\;<\;
(k-1)\,\bigl(m^{\tfrac{k+1}{k}} + 1\bigr)^{k}
\;+\;
(k-1)\,\bigl|V_1\bigr|
\;\le\;
\mathrm{poly}\bigl(k\bigr)\,\bigl(m^{k-1}\bigr).
\]
From this one deduces
\[
\limsup_{m \to \infty}\,\frac{\ln f(m)}{n\,m} \;\le\; \frac{k}{k+1}.
\]

Combining both bounds completes the proof that
\[
\lim_{m \to \infty}\,\frac{\ln f(m)}{n\,m}
\;=\;
\frac{k}{k+1}\,.
\qquad\square
\]

stem_md:
Let  $\varepsilon$  be positive constant and  $u$  satisfies that
\[
\begin{cases} (\partial_t-\varepsilon\partial_x^2-\partial_y^2)u=0, & (t,x,y) \in \mathbb{R}_+ \times \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}_+, \partial_y u\vert_{y=0}=\partial_x h, &u\vert_{t=0}=0. & \end{cases}\]
Here  $h(t,x)$  is a smooth Schwartz function. Define the operator  $e^{a\langle D\rangle}$ \[\mathcal{F}_x(e^{a\langle D\rangle} f)(k)=e^{a\langle k\rangle} \mathcal{F}_x(f)(k), \quad \langle k\rangle=1+\vert k\vert,\]
where  $\mathcal{F}_x$  stands for the Fourier transform in  $x$ . Show that
\[\int_0^T \|e^{(1-s)\langle D\rangle} u\|_{L_{x,y}^2}^2 ds \le C \int_0^T \|e^{(1-s)\langle D\rangle} h\|_{H_x^{\frac{1}{4}}}^2 ds\]
with constant  $C$  independent of  $\varepsilon, T$  and  $h$ .
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/AoPS Yearly Contest Collections/2021 Contests/2021 Alibaba Global Math Competition/2609990.json

candidates:
Note this is equivalent to an \( L^q \)-maximal regularity estimate for the initial boundary value problem. Applying the Fourier transform in the \( x \)-variable to the PDE yields:
\[
\partial_t \hat{u}(t, k, y) - (|k|^2 + \partial_y^2) \hat{u}(t, k, y) = 0,
\]
with the boundary condition in the Fourier domain:
\[
\partial_y \hat{u}(t, k, 0) = i k \hat{h}(t, k),
\]
and the initial condition \( \hat{u}(0, k, y) = 0 \).

Solving this equation yields:
\[
\hat{u}(t, k, y) = \int_0^t e^{-(t-s)(|k|^2 + \partial_y^2)} \partial_y \hat{u}(s, k, 0) \, ds.
\]
Using the boundary condition, this becomes:
\[
\hat{u}(t, k, y) = \int_0^t e^{-(t-s)(|k|^2 + \partial_y^2)} i k \hat{h}(s, k) \, ds.
\]

Applying the operator \( e^{(1-s)\langle D \rangle} \) defined by
\[
\mathcal{F}_x(e^{a \langle D \rangle} f)(k) = e^{a \langle k \rangle} \mathcal{F}_x(f)(k), \quad \langle k \rangle = 1 + |k|,
\]
we have:
\[
e^{(1-s)\langle D \rangle} u(t, x, y) = \mathcal{F}_x^{-1} \left( e^{(1-s)\langle k \rangle} \hat{u}(t, k, y) \right).
\]

We estimate the \( L_{x,y}^2 \) norm of \( e^{(1-s)\langle D \rangle} u \):
\[
\|e^{(1-s)\langle D \rangle} u\|_{L_{x,y}^2}^2 = \int_{\mathbb{R}} \int_{\mathbb{R}_+} |e^{(1-s)\langle k \rangle} \hat{u}(t, k, y)|^2 \, dy \, dk.
\]

Substituting the expression for \( \hat{u}(t, k, y) \) and using Plancherel, we obtain:
\[
\|e^{(1-s)\langle D \rangle} u\|_{L_{x,y}^2}^2 \le \int_0^t \int_{\mathbb{R}} |k|^2 e^{2(1-s)\langle k \rangle} e^{-2(t-s)|k|^2} |\hat{h}(s, k)|^2 \, dk \, ds.
\]

Using the Sobolev space norm equivalence \( \|h\|_{H_x^{\frac{1}{4}}}^2 \sim \int_{\mathbb{R}} (1 + |k|)^{1/2} |\hat{h}(k)|^2 \, dk \), we have:
\[
\|e^{(1-s)\langle D \rangle} u\|_{L_{x,y}^2}^2 \le C \int_0^T \|e^{(1-s)\langle D \rangle} h\|_{H_x^{\frac{1}{4}}}^2 \, ds.
\]
as desired.

stem_md:
Let  $(M,g)$  be an  $n$ -dimensional complete Riemannian manifold with  $n \ge 2$ . Suppose  $M$  is connected and  $\text{Ric} \ge (n-1)g$ , where  $\text{Ric}$  is the Ricci tensor of  $(M,g)$ . Denote by  $\text{d}g$  the Riemannian measure of  $(M,g)$  and by  $d(x,y)$  the geodesic distance between  $x$  and  $y$ . Prove that
\[\int_{M \times M} \cos d(x,y) \text{d}g(x)\text{d}g(y) \ge 0.\]
Moreover, equality holds if and only if  $(M,g)$  is isometric to the unit round sphere  $S^n$ .
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/AoPS Yearly Contest Collections/2021 Contests/2021 Alibaba Global Math Competition/2610000.json

candidates:
hopefully this works

By Bonnet-Myers, \((M, g)\) is compact, and its diameter \(\mathrm{diam}(M)\) satisfies \(\mathrm{diam}(M) \leq \pi\). For all \(x, y \in M\), the geodesic distance \(d(x, y)\) satisfies \(d(x, y) \leq \pi\). The function \(\cos d(x, y)\) is symmetric, as \(d(x, y) = d(y, x)\), and satisfies \(-1 \leq \cos d(x, y) \leq 1\), with \(\cos d(x, y) = -1\) iff. \(d(x, y) = \pi\).

Let \(I = \int_{M \times M} \cos d(x, y) \, \mathrm{d}g(x)\mathrm{d}g(y)\). If \((M, g)\) is not isometric to the unit sphere, then \(\mathrm{diam}(M) < \pi\), implying \(d(x, y) < \pi\) for all \(x, y \in M\). Thus, \(\cos d(x, y) > -1\) everywhere, so the integrand is strictly greater than \(-1\), and so \(I > 0\).

Now consider the case where \(I = 0\), i.e the positive and negative contributions of \(\cos d(x, y)\) cancel exactly. For this to happen, \(\cos d(x, y)\) must attain \(-1\) on a non-trivial subset of \(M \times M\), which implies \(d(x, y) = \pi\) on such a subset. Therefore, \(\mathrm{diam}(M) = \pi\). By Cheng's diameter theorem, if \(\mathrm{diam}(M) = \pi\) and \(\mathrm{Ric} \geq (n-1)g\), then \((M, g)\) must be isometric to the unit round sphere \(S^n\). 

Conversely, if \((M, g)\) is isometric to \(S^n\), consider the integral 

\[
I = \int_{S^n \times S^n} \cos d(x, y) \, \mathrm{d}g(x)\mathrm{d}g(y).
\]

For \(S^n\), the distance \(d(x, y)\) depends only on the angle \(\theta\) between \(x, y \in S^n\). The geodesic distance satisfies \(d(x, y) = \theta\), where \(0 \leq \theta \leq \pi\), and the value of \(\cos d(x, y)\) depends solely on \(\theta\). The measure \(\mathrm{d}g(x)\) is invariant under the group of isometries of \(S^n\), and the symmetry of \(S^n\) ensures that for every pair \(x, y\), there is a corresponding pair \(x', y'\) such that \(\cos d(x, y) = -\cos d(x', y')\). Hence, using this symmetry, the contributions of \(\cos d(x, y)\) for distances in \([0, \pi]\) cancel out in the integral, leading to \(I = 0\). 

Thus, \(I = 0\) if and only if \((M, g)\) is isometric to \(S^n\). Hence

\[
\int_{M \times M} \cos d(x, y) \, \mathrm{d}g(x)\mathrm{d}g(y) \geq 0,
\]

with equality if and only if \((M, g)\) is isometric to the unit round sphere \(S^n\).

stem_md:
Let  $G$  be a finite group, and let  $H_1, H_2 \subset G$  be two subgroups. Suppose that for any representation of  $G$  on a finite-dimensional complex vector space  $V$ , one has that
\[\text{dim} V^{H_1}=\text{dim} V^{H_2},\]
where  $V^{H_i}$  is the subspace of  $H_i$ -invariant vectors in  $V$  ( $i=1,2$ ). Prove that
\[Z(G) \cap H_1=Z(G) \cap H_2.\]
Here  $Z(G)$  denotes the center of  $G$ .
solution_md: For any such representation of  $G$  with character  $\chi$  we have  $\operatorname{dim}V^{H_i}=\langle1,\operatorname{Res}_{H_i}^{G}\chi\rangle_{H_i}=\langle\operatorname{Ind}_{H_i}^{G}1,\chi\rangle_G$ , and so  $\langle\operatorname{Ind}_{H_1}^{G}1,\chi\rangle_G=\langle\operatorname{Ind}_{H_2}^{G}1,\chi\rangle_G$ . Since this holds for every representation of  $G$ , it follows that  $\operatorname{Ind}_{H_1}^{G}1$  and  $\operatorname{Ind}_{H_2}^{G}1$  are equivalent, and thus so are   $\operatorname{Res}_{Z(G)}^{G}\operatorname{Ind}_{H_1}^{G}1$  and  $\operatorname{Res}_{Z(G)}^{G}\operatorname{Ind}_{H_2}^{G}1$ . But kernels of these representations are  $Z(G)\cap H_1$  and  $Z(G)\cap H_2$  respectively (since  $\operatorname{Ind}_{H_i}^{G}1$  is just  $G$  acting on  $G/H_i$  by left multiplication), hence the result.
source_url: aops://metadata/Contest Collections/AoPS Yearly Contest Collections/2021 Contests/2021 Alibaba Global Math Competition/2610003.json

candidates: This may be a silly question, but why is  $\dim V^{H_i} = \langle 1, \text{Res}_{H_i}^G \chi \rangle _{H_i}$ ? I initially thought maybe  $(\text{Res}_{H_i}^G \chi) (h) = \dim V^{H_i}$  for each  $h\in H_i$ , but I realised this is not the case, because note that  $h$  still acts on the whole space  $V$ . So for example,  $\chi (e)$  is still  $\dim V$  instead of  $\dim V^{H_i}$ .

Because both sides are equal to the multiplicity of the trivial representation in the decomposition of  $\text{Res}_{H_i}^G\varphi$  into a sum of irreps, where  $\varphi$  is a representation of  $G$  with character  $\chi$ .

stem_md:
Let  $p$  be a prime number and let  $\mathbb{F}_p$  be the finite field with  $p$  elements. Consider an automorphism  $\tau$  of the polynomial ring  $\mathbb{F}_p[x]$  given by
\[\tau(f)(x)=f(x+1).\]
Let  $R$  denote the subring of  $\mathbb{F}_p[x]$  consisting of those polynomials  $f$  with  $\tau(f)=f$ . Find a polynomial  $g \in \mathbb{F}_p[x]$  such that  $\mathbb{F}_p[x]$  is a free module over  $R$  with basis  $g,\tau(g),\dots,\tau^{p-1}(g)$ .
solution_md:
That's an interesting problem, even though writing the solution is harder than solving the problem! haha

Anyway, I think  $g:=x^{p-1}$  works. To show that   $$ S:=\{(x+i)^{p-1}: \ \ 0 \le i \le p-1\} $$   
generates  $\mathbb{F}_p[x]$  as  $R$ -module, we only need to show that the monomials  $x^n, \ n \ge 0,$  are  $R$ -linear combinations of the elements of  $S.$  But since  $x^n=(x^p-x)x^{n-p}+x^{n-p+1}$  and  $x^p-x \in R,$  we only need to prove that the monomials  $x^n, \  0 \le n \le p-1$  are  $R$ -linear combinations of the elements of  $S.$  So suppose that  $0 \le n \le p-1.$  It suffices to show that there exist  $a_i \in \mathbb{F}_p \subset R$  such that   $$ \sum_{i=0}^{p-1}a_i(x+i)^{p-1} =x^n. $$  Well, consider the polynomial   $$ p_n(x):=\sum_{i=0}^{p-1}a_i(x+i)^{p-1}-x^n, $$  where we want to find  $a_i$  such that  $p_n(x)$  becomes the zero-polynomial. Since  $\deg p_n(x) \le p-1,$  the polynomial  $p_n(x)$  is identically zero if and only if  $p_n(x)=0$  for all  $x \in \mathbb{F}_p.$  If  $n=0,$  we choose  $a_i=-1$  for all  $i$ ; then, since  $x^{p-1} \equiv 1 \mod p$  for all  $0 \ne x \in \mathbb{F}_p,$  we have for all  $x \in \mathbb{F}_p$   $$ p_0(x)=-\sum_{i=0}^{p-1}(x+i)^{p-1}-1=-(p-1)-1 =0 $$  and we're done. If  $n=p-1,$  we obviously choose  $a_0=1$  and  $a_i=0, \ 1 \le i \le p-1.$  For  $1 \le n \le p-2,$  we want to have  $p_n(x)=0$  for  $x=0, 1, \cdots , p-1.$  So for  $x=k, \ 0 \le k \le p-1,$  we have   $$ 0=p_n(k)=\sum_{i=0}^{p-1}a_i(k+i)^{p-1}-k^n=\sum_{i=0}^{p-1}a_i-a_{p-k}-k^n, $$  where we define  $a_p:=a_0.$  Solving the above system gives  $-a_0=\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}k^n=0,$  because  $1 \le n \le p-2,$  and then we get  $a_i=(-1)^{n+1}i^n$  for all  $0 \le i \le p-1.$  So we have proved that  $S$  generates  $\mathbb{F}_p[x].$  

To show that  $S$  is a basis for  $\mathbb{F}_p[x],$  suppose that   $$ \sum_{i=0}^{p-1}r_i(x)(x+i)^{p-1}=0 $$  for some  $r_i(x) \in R.$  We need to show that  $r_i(x)=0$  for all  $i.$  So for all  $0 \le k \le p-1$  we have   $$ \sum_{i=0}^{p-1}r_i(x)\tau^k((x+i)^{p-1})=0, $$  i.e.  $\sum_{i=0}^{p-1}r_i(x)(x+i+k)^{p-1}=0.$  So in terms of matrices, we have  $AX=0,$  where   $$ A=\begin{pmatrix}(x+p-1)^{p-1} & (x+p-2)^{p-1} & \cdots & x^{p-1}  x^{p-1} & (x+p-1)^{p-1} & \cdots & (x+1)^{p-1}  . & . & \cdots & .   . & . & \cdots & .   . & . & \cdots & .  (x+p-2)^{p-1} & (x+p-3)^{p-1} & \cdots & (x+p-1)^{p-1}\end{pmatrix}, \ \ \ \ \ X=\begin{pmatrix}r_{p-1}(x)  r_{p-2}(x)  .  .  .  r_0(x)\end{pmatrix}. $$  Now if we show that  $\det A \ne 0,$  then  $A$  would be invertible in  $\mathbb{F}_p(x)$  and we're done because then  $AX=0$  gives  $X=0.$  So suppose that  $\det A=0,$  i.e. the polynomial  $\det A$  is identically zero. Then we must have  $\det A=0$  for  $x=1$  but that is not true because, for  $x=1,$  the entries of  $A$  on the main diagonal are all zero and all the other entries of  $A$  are  $1$  and it's easy to see that such matrix has non-zero determinant. This contradiction completes the solution.

stem_md:
Let  $p$  be an odd prime number, and let  $m \ge 0$  and  $N \ge 1$  be integers. Let  $\Lambda$  be a free  $\mathbb{Z}/p^N\mathbb{Z}$ -module of rank  $2m+1$ , equipped with a perfect symmetric  $\mathbb{Z}/p^N\mathbb{Z}$ -bilinear form
\[(\, ,\,): \Lambda \times \Lambda \to \mathbb{Z}/p^N\mathbb{Z}.\]
Here ``perfect'' means that the induced map
\[\Lambda \to \text{Hom}_{\mathbb{Z}/p^N\mathbb{Z}}(\Lambda, \mathbb{Z}/p^N\mathbb{Z}), \quad x \mapsto (x,\cdot)\]
is an isomorphism. Find the cardinality of the set
\[\{x \in \Lambda: (x,x)=0\},\]
expressed in terms of  $p,m,N$ .
solution_md:
Let  $\Lambda = (\mathbb{Z}/p^N\mathbb{Z})^{2m+1}$ . The perfect condition implies that the homomorphism  $f(y) = (x,y)$  is nonzero for all  $x\ne 0$  in  $\Lambda$ . 

Consider a matrix  $A_{i,j}=(e_i,e_j). $ **Claim:**this matrix is invertible in  $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$  is a sufficient and necessary condition for "perfect".

Proof: assume the rows are linearly dependent in  $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ . Say there exists constants  $c_1,\cdots, c_{2m+1}$ , not all 0 such that  $\sum c_jr_j=0$  where  $r_j = (r_{j,1}, \cdots, r_{j,n})$ . Then  $(p^{N-1} \sum c_je_j, e_k)=0$  in  $\mathbb{Z}/p^N\mathbb{Z}$  for all  $k=1,\cdots,2m+1$ Work in  $\mathbb{Z}/p^N\mathbb{Z}$  now**Claim:** via an appropriate change of basis  $(e_1,\cdots,e_{2m+1})$  to  $(f_1,\cdots,f_{2m+1})$ , I can get the matrix to be a diagonal matrix (and each cell on the diagonal is not a multiple of p since the matrix remains invertible)

Proof: Consider a process where  $e_1, \cdots, e_{2m+1}$  can change. Let  $S=\{ 1,\cdots, 2m+1\}$ . If for some  $j\notin S$  and  $(e_j,e_j)$  is not a multiple of p for some j, then I can change  $e_k$  to  $e_k - \frac{(e_k,e_j)}{(e_j,e_j)}$  for each  $j\ne k$ . Now  $(e_j, e_k)=0$  for all  $k\ne j$ , and add  $j$  to  $S$ . If  $(e_j,e_j)$  is a multiple of  $p$  for all  $j\in S$ , we find  $k\in S$  such that  $(e_j,e_k)$  is not a multiple of  $p$  (if this is not possible then row  $j$  is the zero vector in  $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$  but the rank of this matrix does not change as  $(e_1,\cdots,e_{2m+1})$  remains a basis of  $\Lambda$ .  Replace  $e_j$  with  $e_j+e_k$  and note  $(e_j+e_k, e_j+e_k)=2(e_j,e_k)$  by symmetry, which is not a multiple of  $p$ . 
In this process, when any number  $s$  is inserted to  $S$  we have  $(e_s,e_t)=0$  in  $\mathbb{Z}/p^N\mathbb{Z}$ Therefore, the matrix is eventually diagonal. If  $c_s=(e_s,e_s)$ , if  $x=\sum_{j=1}^{2m+1} x_je_j$  for some  $x_j\in \mathbb{Z}/p^N\mathbb{Z}$  then  $(x,x)=\sum_{j=1}^{2m+1} c_jx_j^2$ Let f(N) be the answer for N. Note that  $f(0)=1, f(1)=p^{2m}$  can be proven via Gauss Sums.

The key observation is to note that among all  $x_1,\cdots,x_{2m+1}$  when  $p\mid \sum_{j=1}^{2m+1} c_jx_j^2$  and  $p$  doesn't divide one of them, the residue of  $\sum_{j=1}^{2m+1} c_jx_j^2$  mod  $p^N$  takes on each multiple of  $p$  the same number of times. 

Proof of key observation: let  $j$  be the smallest number  $j$  such that  $p\nmid x_j$ . Put in the group  $\{ (x_1,\cdots,x_{j-1},x_j+kp,x_{j+1},\cdots, x_n) \mid k=0,\cdots,p^N-1 \}$ . We can see that for any residue r mod  $p^N$  that is a multiple of  $p$ , there are exactly  $p$  k's that satisfy  $T(k)=\sum_{1\le l \le 2m+1, l\ne j} c_lx_l^2 + c_j(x_j+kp)^2 \equiv r (\bmod\; p^N)$ , because  $T(a)=T(b)$  iff  $p^{N-1}\mid a-b$ .

We go back to computing  $f(N)$ . 
When  $p$  divides  $x_1,\cdots,x_{2m+1}$ , we need  $p^{N-2} \mid \sum c_k(x_k/p)^2$  where  $x_k/p\in \mathbb{Z}/p^{N-1}\mathbb{Z}$ . This gives  $f(N-2) p^{2m+1}$  possibilities because for each of the  $f(N-2)$  possibilities with each  $x_j/p$  in  $\{0,\cdots,p^{N-2}-1\}$  there are  $p$  ways to add a multiple of  $p^{N-2}$  to each  $x_j/p$ When p doesn't divide one of  $x_1,\cdots,x_{2m+1}$ , then the number of  $(x_1,\cdots,x_{2m+1})$  satisfying  $p^N\mid \sum c_kx_k^2$  is  $p^{-N+1}$  times the number of  $(x_1,\cdots,x_{2m+1})$  satisfying  $p\mid c_kx_k^2$ . The latter can be found to be  $p^{(2m+1)N-1}-p^{(2m+1)(N-1)}$ Therefore  $f(N)=p^{2mN} - p^{2m(N-1)} + p^{2m+1} f(N-2)$ . Via induction it is easy to prove that   $$ f(2k) = p^{4km} + (p-1) \frac{p^{4km-1}-p^{(2m+1)k-1}}{p^{2m-1}-1} $$    $$ f(2k+1) = p^{2m} ( p^{4km} + (p-1) \frac{p^{4km-1}-p^{(2m+1)k-1}}{p^{2m-1}-1}) $$

For the complex-valued function  $f(x)$  which is continuous and absolutely integrable on  $\mathbb{R}$ , define the function  $(Sf)(x)$  on  $\mathbb{R}$ :  $(Sf)(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}e^{2\pi iux}f(u)du$ .
(a) Find the expression for  $S(\frac{1}{1+x^2})$  and  $S(\frac{1}{(1+x^2)^2})$ .
(b) For any integer  $k$ , let  $f_k(x)=(1+x^2)^{-1-k}$ . Assume  $k\geq 1$ , find constant  $c_1$ ,  $c_2$  such that the function  $y=(Sf_k)(x)$  satisfies the ODE with second order:  $xy''+c_1y'+c_2xy=0$ .
solution_md:
For (b), (I am changing some variables)

<details><summary>Solution</summary>Notice that  $y(t)=\int_{-\infty}^\infty \frac{\cos(2\pi tx)}{(1+x^2)^{1+n}} \ \mathrm dx$ . We find  $y'(t)=-2\pi \int_{-\infty}^\infty \frac{x\sin (2\pi tx)}{(1+x^2)^{1+n}} \ \mathrm dx$  and   $$ y''(t)=-4\pi^2\int_{-\infty}^\infty \frac{x^2\cos(2\pi tx)}{(1+x^2)^{1+n}} \ \mathrm dx=-4\pi^2 \int_{-\infty}^\infty \cos(2\pi tx)\left(\frac{1}{(1+x^2)^n}-\frac{1}{(1+x^2)^{1+n}} \right) \ \mathrm dx. $$   Now with IBP   $$ \int_{-\infty}^\infty \frac{\cos(2\pi tx)}{(1+x^2)^n} \ \mathrm dx=\frac{\sin(2\pi tx)}{2\pi t(1+x^2)^n} \Big\vert_{-\infty}^\infty +\frac{n}{\pi t} \int_{-\infty}^\infty \frac{x\sin (2\pi tx)}{(1+x^2)^{1+n}} \ \mathrm dx=-\frac{n}{2\pi^2 t} y'(t). $$   Hence  $y''(t)=\frac{2n}t y'(t)+4\pi^2 y(t)$ . So  $\boxed{(c_1,c_2)=(-2n,-4\pi^2)}$ .</details>

Now to evaluate the integrals themselves it remains to solve the ODE:  $ty''(t)-2ny'(t)-4\pi^2 t y(t)=0$  with some  $y(0),y'(0)$  derivable from the integrals. I think series (in particular, Frobenius method) should work.

The statement is very artificial and I do not see its interest; but it is difficult to solve.
According to my above post,  $Y$  has  $7$  distinct eigenvalues iff  $rank(A)=3$  and  $AA^T$  has  $3$  distinct eigenvalues. 
We put  $b_i=a_i^2$ , where the  $b_i$  are  $>0$  and distinct.
Let  $\sigma_i,i=1\cdots 4$  be the elementary symmetric polynomials of the  $b_i$  (for example  $\sigma_2=\sum_{i<j}b_ib_j$ ). Note that  $\sigma_i>0$ .
Up to a factor,  $\chi_{AA^T}(x)=\sigma_1x^3-2\sigma_2x^2+3\sigma_3x-4\sigma_4$  and has  $3$   $>0$  roots (because the singular values of  $A$  are  $\geq 0$  and  $\sigma_4>0$ ); then,  $\delta=discrim(\chi_{AA^T})=-432\sigma_1^2\sigma_4^2+432\sigma_1\sigma_2\sigma_3\sigma_4-108\sigma_1\sigma_3^3-128\sigma_2^3\sigma_4+36\sigma_2^2\sigma_3^2\geq 0$ .
Note that  $\delta$  is an homogeneous polynomial of degree  $10$  in the  $b_i$ ; since we want to show that  $\delta >0$ , we may assume that  $\sigma_2=1$ .
We seek  $\min(\delta)$ ; by canceling the partial derivatives of  $\delta$  wrt   $\sigma_1,\sigma_3,\sigma_4$ , we obtain  ${\sigma}_2=1,{\sigma}_3=\dfrac{12}{27\sigma_1},{\sigma}_4=\dfrac{2}{27{\sigma}_1^2}$  and, for all these  candidates, the associated value of  $\delta$  is  $0$ .
We come back to the  $b_i$ , adding the conditions "the  $b_i$  are  $> 0$  and distinct".  We obtain conditions in the form $(3b_1^3b_2+6b_1^2b_2^2+3b_1b_2^3-b_1^2-b_2^2)
(9b_1^6b_2^2+18b_1^4b_2^4+9b_1^2b_2^6-6b_1^5b_2+12b_1^4b_2^2-24b_1^3b_2^3+12b_1^2b_2^4-6b_1b_2^5+2b_1^4-6b_1^3b_2+9b_1^2b_2^2-6b_1b_2^3+2b_2^4)=0$ The second factor is  $0$  for  $b_1\geq 0,b_2\geq 0$  only when  $b_1=b_2=0$ . Then  $3b_1^3b_2+6b_1^2b_2^2+3b_1b_2^3-b_1^2-b_2^2=0$  and -by symmetry- the  $5$  other relations obtained by grouping the  $b_i$  in pairs.
These  $6$  relations imply -for example- that  $b_1=b_3$  or  $b_1=0$  , a contradiction. 
Since  $\delta=0$  is not reached,  $\delta>0$  and we are done.   $\square$

Note: AGMC means Alibaba Global Math Contest. Very interesting solution by loup blanc. Here is my solution to (a) via block multiplication.
Let $Y= \begin{bmatrix} 0_n&A A^T&0_{n+1} \end{bmatrix}$ For some $n\times (n+1)$ matrix $A$ , define $P(\lambda)=\det(Y-\lambda I), Q(\lambda)=\det(AA^T-\lambda I)$ . Prove that $P(x)=x Q(x^2)$ .
Essentially, we want to show that $$ \det(Y-xI_{2n+1}) = x \det(AA^T-x^2I_n) $$ $$ \begin{bmatrix}I_n&\frac{1}{x}A 0&I_{n+1}\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}-xI_n&A A^T&-xI_{n+1} \end{bmatrix} =\begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{x}AA^T-xI_n&0 A^T&-xI_{n+1} \end{bmatrix} $$ Here we used a technique called blocking. Note we can think of this as multiplying a $2\times 2$ matrix of matrices. Note $$ det\begin{bmatrix}I_n&\frac{1}{x}A 0&I_{n+1}\end{bmatrix}=1 $$ If I use the permutation definition of the determinant then to make the product of terms zero one must choose $\sigma=id$ . By definition, $$ det\begin{bmatrix}-xI_n&A A^T&-xI_{n+1} \end{bmatrix}=det(Y-xI_{2n+1}) $$ Finally, $$ det\begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{x}AA^T-xI_n&0 A^T&-xI_{n+1} \end{bmatrix} = det(\frac{1}{x} AA^T-xI_n) (-x)^{n+1} $$ When we choose a permutation $\sigma: [2n+1] \to [2n+1]$ we need $a_{i,\sigma(i)}\ne 0$ . Then $\sigma(j) \le n$ for all $j\le n$ so $\sigma(j)=j$ for all $j\in \{n+1,\cdots,2n+1\}$ . Therefore, the equation holds. Now rearranging yields the desired result.

The winners of first AGMC in 2019 gifts the person in charge of the organiser, which is a polyhedron formed by  $60$  congruent triangles. From the photo, we can see that this polyhedron formed by  $60$  quadrilateral spaces.
(Note: You can find the photo in 3.4 of [https://files.alicdn.com/tpsservice/18c5c7b31a7074edc58abb48175ae4c3.pdf?spm=a1zmmc.index.0.0.51c0719dNAbw3C&file=18c5c7b31a7074edc58abb48175ae4c3.pdf](https://files.alicdn.com/tpsservice/18c5c7b31a7074edc58abb48175ae4c3.pdf?spm=a1zmmc.index.0.0.51c0719dNAbw3C&file=18c5c7b31a7074edc58abb48175ae4c3.pdf))
A quadrilateral space is the plane figures that we fold the figures following the diagonal on a  $n$  sides on a plane (i.e. form an appropriate dihedral angle in where the chosen diagonal is). "Two figure spaces are congruent" means they can coincide completely by isometric transform in  $\mathbb{R}^3$ . A polyhedron is the bounded space region, whose boundary is formed by the common edge of finite polygon.
(a) We know that  $2021=43\times 47$ . Does there exist a polyhedron, whose surface can be formed by  $43$  congruent  $47$ -gon?
(b) Prove your answer in (a) with logical explanation.

stem_md:
When a company releases a new social media software, the marketing development of the company researches and analyses the characteristics of the customer group apart from paying attention to the active customer depending on the change of the time. We use  $n(t, x)$  to express the customer density (which will be abbreviated as density). Here  $t$  is the time and  $x$  is the time of the customer spent on the social media software. In the instant time  $t$ , for  $0<x_1<x_2$ , the number of customers of spending time between  $x_1$  and  $x_2$  is  $\int_{x_1}^{x_2}n(t,x)dx$ . We assume the density  $n(t,x)$  depends on the time and the following factors:
Assumption 1. When the customer keeps using that social media software, their time spent on social media increases linearly.
Assumption 2. During the time that the customer uses the social media software, they may stop using it. We assumption the speed of stopping using it  $d(x)>0$  only depends on  $x$ .
Assumption 3. There are two sources of new customer.
(i) The promotion from the company: A function of time that expresses the increase of number of people in a time unit, expressed by  $c(t)$ .
(ii) The promotion from previous customer: Previous customer actively promotes this social media software to their colleagues and friends actively. The speed of promoting sucessfully depends on  $x$ , denoted as  $b(x)$ .
Assume if in an instant time, denoted as  $t=0$ , the density function is known and  $n(0,x)=n_0(x)$ . We can derive. The change of time  $n(t,x)$  can satisfy the equation: $\begin{cases}
\frac{\partial}{\partial t}n(t,x)+\frac{\partial}{\partial x}n(t,x)+d(x)n(t,x)=0, t\ge 0, x\ge 0

N(t):=n(t,x=0)=c(t)+\int_{0}^{\infty}b(y)n(t,y)dy
    \end{cases}\,$ where  $N(t)$  iis the speed of the increase of new customers. We assume  $b, d \in L^\infty_-(0, \infty)$ .  $b(x)$  and  $d(x)$  is bounded in essence. The following, we first make a simplified assumption:  $c(t)\equiv 0$ , i.e. the increase of new customer depends only on the promotion of previous customer.
(a) According to assumption 1 and 2, formally derive the PDE that  $n(t, x)$  satisfies in the two simtaneous equation above. You are required to show the assumption of model and the relationship between the Maths expression. Furthermore, according to assumption 3, explain the definition and meaning of  $N(t)$  in the simtaneous equation above.
(b) We want to research the relationship of the speed of the increase of the new customers  $N(t)$  and the speed of promoting sucessfully  $b(x)$ . Derive an equation that  $N(t)$  satisfies in terms of  $N(t), n_0(x), b(x), d(x)$  only and does not include  $n(t, x)$ . Prove that  $N(t)$  satifies the estimation  $|N(t)|\le ||b||_\infty e^{||b||_\infty t}\int_{0}^{\infty}|n_0(x)|dx$ , where  $||\cdot||_\infty$  is the norm of  $L^\infty$ .
(c) Finally, we want to research, after sufficiently long time, what trend of number density function  $n(t, x) $ \frac{d} has. As the total number of customers may keep increasing so it is not comfortable for us to research the number density function  $n(t, x)$ . We should try to find a density function which is renormalized. Hence, we first assume there is one only solution  $(\lambda_0,\varphi(x))$  of the following eigenvalue problem: $\begin{cases}
\varphi'(x)+(\lambda_0+d(x))\varphi(x)=0, x\ge 0

\varphi(x)>0,\varphi(0)=\int_{0}^{\infty}b(x)\varphi(x)dx=1
    \end{cases}\,
$ and its dual problem has only solution  $\psi(x)$ : $\begin{cases}
-\varphi'(x)+(\lambda_0+d(x))\psi(x)=\psi(0)b(x), x\ge 0

\psi(x)>0,\int_{0}^{\infty}\psi(x)\varphi(x)dx=1
    \end{cases}\,$ Prove that for any convex function  $H:\mathbb{R}^+\to \mathbb{R}^+$  which satisfies  $H(0)=0$ . We have $\frac{d}{dx}\int_{0}^{\infty}\psi(x)\varphi(x)H(\frac{\tilde{n}(t,x)}{\varphi(x)})dx\le 0, \forall t\ge 0$ .
Furthermore, prove that  $\int_{0}^{\infty}\psi(x)n(t,x)dx=e^{\lambda_0t}\int_{0}^{\infty}\psi(x)n_0(x)dx$ To simplify the proof, the contribution of boundary terms in  $\infty$  is negligible.

stem_md:
Last year, Master Cheung is famous for multi-rotation. This year, he comes to DAMO to make noodles for sweeping monk. One day, software engineer Xiao Li talks with Master Cheung about his job. Xiao Li mainly researches and designs the algorithm to adjust the paramter of different kinds of products. These paramters can normally be obtainly by minimising loss function  $f$  on  $\mathbb{R}^n$ . In the recent project of Xiao Li, this loss function is obtained by other topics. For safety consideration and technique reasons, this topic makes Xiao Li difficult to find the interal details of the function. They only provide a port to calculate the value of  $f(\text x)$  for any  $\text x\in\mathbb{R}^n$ . Therefore, Xiao Li must only use the value of the function to minimise  $f$ . Also, every times calculating the value of  $f$  will use a lot of calculating resources. It is good to know that the dimension  $n$  is not very high (around  $10$ ). Also, colleague who provides the function tells Xiao Li to assume  $f$  is smooth first.
This problem reminds Master Cheung of his antique radio. If you want to hear a programme from the radio, you need to turn the knob of the radio carefully. At the same time, you need to pay attention to the quality of the radio received, until the quality is the best. In this process, no one knows the relationship between the angle of turning the knob and the quality of the radio received. Master Cheung and Xiao Li realizes that minimising  $f$  is same as adjusting the machine with multiple knobs: Assume every weight of  $\text x$  is controlled by a knob.  $f(\text x)$  is a certain performance of the machine. We only need to adjust every knobs again and again and observes the value of  $f$  in the same time. Maybe there is hope to find the best  $\text x$ . As a result, two people suggest an iteration algorithm (named Automated Forward/Backward Tuning,  $\text{AFBT}$ , to minimise  $f$ . In  $k$ -th iteration, the algorithm adjusts the individual weight of  $\text{x}_k$  to  $2n$  points  $\{\text x_k\pm t_k\text e^i:i=1,...,n\}$ , where  $t_k$  is the step size; then, make  $y_k$  be the smallest one among the value of the function of thosse points. Then check if  $\text y_k$  sufficiently makes  $f$  decrease; then, take  $\text x_{k+1}=\text y_k$ , then make the step size doubled. Otherwise, make  $\text x_{k+1}=\text x_k$  and makes the step size decrease in half. In the algorithm,  $\text e^i$  is the  $i$ -th coordinate vector in  $\mathbb{R}^n$ . The weight of  $i$ -th is  $1$ . Others are  $0$ ;  $\mathbf{1}(\cdot)$  is indicator function. If  $f(\text x_k)-f(\text y_k)$  is at least the square of  $t_k$ , then take the value of  $\mathbf{1}(f(\text k)-f(y_k)\ge t^2_k)$  as  $1$ . Otherwise, take it as  $0$ . $\text{AFBT}$  algorithm
Input  $\text{x}_0\in \mathbb{R}^n$ ,  $t_0>0$ . For  $k=0, 1, 2, ...$ , perform the following loop:
1: #Calculate loss function.
2:  $s_k:=\mathbb{1}[f(\text{x}_k)-f(\text{y}_k)\ge t^2_k]$  #Is it sufficiently decreasing? Yes:  $s_k=1$ ; No:  $s_k=0$ .
3:  $\text{x}_{k+1}:=(1-s_k)\text{x}_k+s_k\text{y}_k$  #Update the point of iteration.
4:  $t_{k+1}:=2^{2S_k-1}t_k$  #Update step size.  $s_k=1$ : Step size doubles;  $s_k=0$ : Step size decreases by half.

Now, we made assumption to the loss function  $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to \mathbb{R}$ .
Assumption 1. Let  $f$  be a convex function. For any  $\text{x}, \text{y}\in \mathbb{R}^n$  and  $\alpha \in [0, 1]$ , we have  $f((1-\alpha)\text{x}+\text{y})\le (1-\alpha)f(\text{x})+\alpha f(\text{y})$ .
Assumption 2.  $f$  is differentiable on  $\mathbb{R}^n$  and  $\nabla f$  is L-Lipschitz continuous on  $\mathbb{R}^n$ .
Assumption 3. The level set of  $f$  is bounded. For any  $\lambda\in\mathbb{R}$ , set  $\{\text x\in \mathbb{R}^n:f(\text x)\le \lambda\}$  is all bounded.
Based on assumption 1 and 2, we can prove that  $\left\langle \nabla f(\text x),\text y-\text x \right\rangle \le f(\text y)-f(\text x)\le \left\langle \nabla f(\text x),\text y-\text x\right\rangle+\frac{L}{2}||\text x-\text y||^2$ You can refer to any convex analysis textbook for more properties of convex function.
Prove that under the assumption 1-3, for  $AFBT$ ,  $\lim_{k \to \infty}f(\text{x}_k)=f^*$

stem_md: On a circle there're  $1000$  marked points, each colored in one of  $k$  colors. It's known that among any  $5$  pairwise intersecting segments, endpoints of which are  $10$  distinct marked points, there're at least  $3$  segments, each of which has its endpoints colored in different colors. Determine the smallest possible value of  $k$  for which it's possible.
solution_md:
@above Am I getting the question wrong or something, or you are wrong? We claim that $k=143$ is the minimum value that $k$ can take. Indeed, if $k\leq 142$ , then by pigeonhole there exist a color which is used at least $8$ times. WLOG let those points be $A_1 , A_2 , \dots , A_8$ in clockwise order and let there be at least $2$ points between $A_1$ and $A_8$ . But then taking the segments $A_1A_6$ , $A_2A_7$ , $A_3A_8$ , $A_4A_i$ , $A_5A_j$ (Where $A_i , A_j$ are between $A_1$ and $A_8$ and $A_i$ is closer to $A_8$ then $A_j$ ) gives us a contradiction because there are only $2$ segments each of which has its endpoints colored in different colors. To see that $k=143$ works you can see the attachment. (Colors from $1$ upto $142$ are used $7$ times and color $143$ is used $6$ times.)

Also, for any 2 distinct points  $A, B$  which have at least 4 points between them (both clockwise and anticlockwise), you can always find 4 other segments which are pairwise intersecting. 

Hence, if we label the points  $A_1, A_2, \cdots A_{1000}$  in order, then  $A_i, A_j$  can't have the same color if there are less than 4 points between them in either direction, and further,  $A_i, A_j$  can always have the same color if there are at least 4 points between them in both directions, so we may colour  $A_i, A_{i+1}, A_{i+2}, A_{i+3}, A_{i+4}$  the same color, and no other point may have the same color. So there are at least  $\frac{1000}{5} = 200$  colors used.
